With brief introduction on gender equality, discuss the following. a. Why gender balance is required? b. Discuss various initiatives taken by the government of India and the international maritime organisation towards gender equality in shipping. c. How would you as the Chief engineer of a ship which has women seafarers ensure that these initiatives have the desired impact? (16)

blocks.h: 1. What gender equality means at sea, and what the goal actually says

blocks.p: The United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development sets seventeen goals, of which the one the question quotes is to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls. Applied to shipping, gender equality does not mean pretending that the ship is a neutral place. It means that a seafarer's access to the job, to training, to promotion and to a safe working and living environment does not depend on her sex - and, because a ship is also a home, that the accommodation, the sanitary arrangements, the medical provision and the behavioural standards on board are fit for a mixed crew rather than merely tolerable to a minority within it.

Two distinctions are worth making at the outset, because the rest of the answer depends on them. First, equality of opportunity is not the same as equality of outcome: the obligation is to remove barriers, not to guarantee proportions. Second - and this is the point the examiner is really testing - gender balance is an aspiration, but non-discrimination is already law. Under the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 each Member must satisfy itself that its law respects the fundamental right to the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation, and every seafarer has the right to a safe and secure workplace and to decent working and living conditions on board. Those are binding obligations that reach the ship whether or not any programme exists.

ul: It is a matter of right, not of favour. Excluding half the population from a profession is discrimination in respect of employment and occupation, which the Convention's own fundamental rights article requires each Member to eliminate. That is the first and sufficient reason, and it does not depend on any business case.

The industry needs the people. Shipping recruits officers from a shrinking pool and competes with shore employment that offers a normal domestic life. A profession that draws from half its potential workforce is choosing to make its own shortage worse.

Selection from a wider pool raises quality. If the best candidate for a fourth engineer's berth is excluded before she applies, the berth is filled by someone less good. This is a straightforward consequence of restricting the field and it holds regardless of any argument about aptitude.

Mixed teams manage risk differently. A crew whose members share one background tends also to share its blind spots, and the human-element failures behind most casualties - unchallenged authority, poor communication, reluctance to speak up - are exactly the failures a more varied team is less prone to. This is an argument about diversity of perspective, not about the qualities of either sex, and it should be put that way.

Retention. Recruiting women and then losing them within a contract or two is more expensive than not recruiting them. Retention depends on the conditions on board, which is precisely what limb (c) is about.

It is now a commercial expectation. Charterers, financiers, insurers and terminal operators increasingly ask about the social element of an operator's practice, and a policy that cannot be evidenced is a commercial exposure as well as an ethical one.

It changes the profession's own standards. Accommodation, sanitary arrangements, personal protective equipment sizing, medical provision and shipboard behaviour all improve for everyone when they are designed for a mixed crew instead of assumed for a single one.

blocks.p: One caution belongs here, and it is worth a mark in itself: the case does not need to be exaggerated. Figures for the proportion of women in the world seafaring workforce are widely quoted and vary considerably between sources. This answer quotes none, because an unsourced statistic in an examination script is a liability, and the argument above stands without one.

blocks.h: 3. What the International Maritime Organization does

blocks.p: The Organization's work on this is programme work rather than regulation. It has no convention on gender, and it does not certify a ship for it. What it does, through its technical cooperation function, is build the supply of qualified women and make the profession visible to them:

ul: a long-standing women in maritime programme under the Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme, aimed at access to maritime training and to positions in maritime administrations;
support for regional women in maritime associations, which give a professional network across national administrations and industry in each region;
fellowships and reserved places for women at the Organization's own academic institutions, including the World Maritime University and the International Maritime Law Institute;
a World Maritime Day theme devoted to women in the maritime community, used to put the subject in front of Member States and industry for a full year;

gender-parity mechanisms written into ordinary technical programmes, which is the most durable form because it does not depend on a separate initiative. A worked example can be given from an instrument that has nothing to do with gender at all: the Organization's GHG-SMART capacity-building programme, described in the appendix to the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, provides for two trainees - one female and one male - to go on to a World Maritime University scholarship.
the same Strategy's insistence that the human element and the impact on seafarers be addressed in the energy transition, which is where the next generation of shipboard jobs will be created.

blocks.p: What is deliberately not said: no resolution number is given for any of this. The Organization has adopted instruments touching the subject, but no licensed text of one is held for this answer, and inventing a number to look authoritative is precisely the error that costs marks in the oral.

blocks.h: 4. What the Government of India does

blocks.p: India's maritime administration is the Directorate General of Shipping, acting under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which is the statute in force at this sitting. Its instruments are the ordinary administrative ones - training and examination rules, certification requirements, approval of maritime training institutes, and notices to the industry. The measures relevant here operate at that level:

ul: Admission to training on the same terms. Women are admitted to approved Indian maritime training institutes and to the pre-sea and post-sea courses that lead to certificates of competency, in the engineering as well as the nautical stream.

Certification and service in all departments and ranks. Eligibility for a certificate of competency and for shipboard service is not restricted by sex, so there is no legal barrier to a woman holding the Chief Engineer's certificate this examination leads to.

Conditions attached to institute approval. The administration's approval regime for training institutes is the practical lever - separate accommodation and sanitary facilities, safeguarding requirements and complaint mechanisms are conditions of running a course, not aspirations.

Berth and cadet-training availability. The recurring practical obstacle for an Indian cadet is not admission but obtaining a training berth, and administration and industry pressure on shipowners to provide them is where policy meets reality.

Implementation of the Maritime Labour Convention through national law. India's ratification carries the Article III and Article IV obligations into the domestic regime, which is what gives a woman seafarer on an Indian ship an enforceable position rather than a policy statement.
Promotion and visibility - recognition of women officers, participation in the regional women in maritime association, and encouragement of shipowners to recruit and retain women.

blocks.p: Again, no circular, rule, notice or scheme number is asserted here. The administration issues numbered instruments and a candidate who has one in front of him should cite it; one who does not should describe the measure and say what it does, which scores, rather than invent a number, which does not.

blocks.h: 5. The obligations that already bind the ship

blocks.p: Before any initiative, the Chief Engineer is already working to binding requirements, and quoting them is what turns limb (c) from good intentions into a management answer:

rows: MLC Article III(d)
Each Member's law must respect the fundamental right to the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation
MLC Article IV
Every seafarer has the right to a safe and secure workplace, to fair terms of employment, and to decent working and living conditions on board
MLC Standard A3.1
On ships other than passenger ships, an individual sleeping room for each seafarer, which removes at a stroke most of the accommodation objection historically raised against mixed crews
MLC Guideline B4.3.1

National occupational safety and health provisions should address harassment, taking account of the industry Guidance on eliminating shipboard harassment and bullying jointly published by the shipowners' and seafarers' international organisations. Harassment is an OSH matter, not a matter of manners
MLC Regulation 5.1.5 / Standard A5.1.5

A fair, effective and expeditious on-board complaint procedure; victimization prohibited and penalized; resolution at the lowest level but the right to go directly to the master and to external authorities preserved; the right to be accompanied; and every seafarer given the procedure, the flag State and home-country contacts, and the name of a person on board who can give confidential impartial advice

blocks.h: 6. As Chief Engineer - the physical ship

ul: Accommodation and sanitary arrangements. Confirm before the crew joins that the individual cabin required by the Convention is in fact allocated and lockable, and that private, secure sanitary facilities are available. If the arrangement depends on sharing, it is my problem to solve before arrival, not hers to raise afterwards.

Personal protective equipment that fits. Boiler suits, gloves, safety shoes, harnesses, breathing apparatus face masks and immersion suits stocked in the full range of sizes. Ill-fitting PPE is a direct safety failure and it is the most common, most visible and most easily corrected signal that a ship was not expecting her.

Workshop and machinery-space practicalities. Lifting aids and correct tooling used as routine rather than as a concession, so that no job in the engine room is done by main force alone. This is good practice for every engineer and it removes the argument before it is made.
Medical provision. Ensure the medical locker and the ship's medical arrangements match the crew actually carried, and that the confidentiality of medical matters is real.
Safety equipment sizing checked in drills, not assumed from the inventory.

blocks.h: 7. As Chief Engineer - work, watches and training

ul: Allocate work by rank and competence, and by nothing else. The single most damaging thing a Chief Engineer can do is protect a woman engineer from the dirty or heavy jobs. It looks like consideration; it is exclusion, it destroys her credibility with the ratings, and it leaves her under-trained for her next certificate.
Give the same watch and project responsibility - the same overhauls, the same faults to diagnose, the same responsibility for a survey item - and hold it to the same standard.
Appraise honestly. Feedback withheld for fear of appearing harsh is the quiet way careers are ended. She is entitled to the same correction as anyone else and to the same record of her competence.

Mentor, and be seen to. A cadet or junior engineer who is the only woman on board has no peer to ask. Deliberate, planned time on machinery and on certificate preparation costs little and is what converts recruitment into retention.
Include her in the department's decisions - planned maintenance, the repair list, the pre-arrival plan - so that authority follows the rank rather than the individual.
Watch the workload distribution in the hours of rest records: a junior who is given every awkward job, or excluded from every desirable one, will show up there before she says anything.

blocks.h: 8. As Chief Engineer - behaviour, complaints and accountability

ul: Set the standard explicitly and early. At the departmental meeting on joining, state what is expected and what will not be tolerated - not as a policy reading, but as an instruction from the head of department. The standard on a ship is whatever the senior officers visibly accept.
Deal with the first incident, however small. A remark left uncorrected is a permission. Correcting it once, immediately and privately, prevents almost everything that would otherwise follow.

Make the complaint route real. Ensure every member of the department has the on-board complaint procedure, knows who the impartial adviser is, and knows that the right to go to the master or to an external authority is not affected by raising it with me first.

Protect the complainant. Victimization is prohibited and penalized under the Convention. If a complaint is raised, my job is to ensure that nothing changes in her work allocation, her appraisal or her treatment because of it - and to be seen to ensure it.

Treat harassment as an OSH matter, which is what the Convention's own guideline makes it: risk-assess it, address it in the safety committee, and record it like any other hazard rather than handling it privately as a personality problem.

Use the safety management system. Report and record under the SMS so that the Company and the DPA see the pattern, and so that the response does not depend on which Chief Engineer happens to be aboard.
Brief the reliefs. Standards that survive one contract and lapse at the next are not standards. Hand over the department's expectations as deliberately as the machinery condition.
Be careful with visibility. Singling someone out as an example is as isolating as ignoring her. The objective is that within a few weeks she is simply the fourth engineer.

blocks.p: The honest summary is that the initiatives in limb (b) can only get a woman to the gangway. Whether she stays in the profession is decided almost entirely by what happens in the six months after she walks up it, and in the engine room that is decided by the Chief Engineer.

This looks like an easy question and is not. It is easy to fill a page with sentiment and score four marks out of sixteen. The marks are in three quite different places: an argued case in limb (a), specific initiatives in limb (b), and a practical, ship-level programme in limb (c). Limb (c) is the one addressed to the candidate personally and it is where an examiner looks for original thought, so it should get at least a third of the writing.

The prize move on this question is to anchor it in the Maritime Labour Convention. Almost every script treats gender equality as a matter of policy and goodwill; a script that says non-discrimination is a fundamental right under Article III, that harassment is an occupational safety and health matter under Guideline B4.3.1, and that victimization of a complainant is prohibited under Standard A5.1.5, has moved the whole answer from opinion to obligation. That is a management-level answer and it is what the marks are for.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb (c) write itself

blocks.p: Initiatives recruit; conditions retain. Everything in limb (b) is about getting a woman to the gangway - training places, fellowships, certification access, visibility. None of it has any effect on whether she is still at sea in three years. That is decided by the cabin, the boiler suit that fits, the overhaul she is trusted with, and whether the first inappropriate remark was corrected or laughed at. Say that once and the whole of limb (c) follows from it in the right order: the ship, the work, the behaviour.

ul: Quoting a percentage. Figures for women as a share of the seafaring workforce are widely repeated and vary between sources. An unsourced number in a script invites the one oral question you cannot answer. The argument does not need it.
Inventing a resolution or circular number to look authoritative. If you have one, cite it; if not, describe the measure and what it does. A named measure with no number scores; a wrong number costs.

Writing limb (c) as a list of good intentions - 'I will treat everyone equally'. The marks are in specific, checkable actions: PPE sizing, cabin allocation, work allocation by rank, the named impartial adviser, the SMS report.
Protective allocation. Writing that you would keep her off the heavy or dirty jobs. It reads as considerate and is in fact the discrimination the question is about.
Treating harassment as a matter of shipboard manners. Under the Convention's own guideline it belongs in the occupational safety and health regime.
Answering limb (b) for only one of the two bodies. The stem asks about the Government of India and the Organization, and half an answer is half the marks.
Ignoring the introduction the stem asks for. It says 'with brief introduction on gender equality' - one short paragraph, not a page.

The printed marks. This question prints no per-limb marks - a single (16) sits at the end of limb c. Do not invent a split and do not assume the limbs are equal in effort; give limb (c) the most writing because it is the one that asks for your own judgement.
The Indian statute. At this sitting the governing Act is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, twenty months after this paper, and must not appear.
The SDG number. The goal the stem quotes is the gender equality goal; do not confuse it with the climate goal the IMO cites in its GHG work.

Being asked in the oral 'what does MLC actually require you to provide?' The answer is the individual sleeping room on a cargo ship under Standard A3.1, the safe and secure workplace under Article IV, and the complaint procedure with its impartial adviser under Standard A5.1.5.

Being asked 'what would you do if a complaint was made against a senior officer?' The procedure resolves at the lowest level possible, but the seafarer's right to go directly to the master and to external authorities is preserved, and victimization is prohibited and penalized.
Which Convention makes non-discrimination a fundamental right for seafarers? MLC 2006, Article III(d) - the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation.

Where does harassment sit in the Convention? In occupational safety and health, through Guideline B4.3.1, which also directs attention to the jointly published industry guidance on eliminating shipboard harassment and bullying.

What does the Convention say about a seafarer who complains? Victimization is prohibited and penalized, and every seafarer is given the procedure, the flag State and home-country contacts, and the name of an impartial adviser on board.
Name one concrete thing you would change before a woman engineer joins. PPE in the correct sizes, and confirmation that the individual cabin and private sanitary facilities are in fact allocated.
Why is protecting her from heavy work wrong? It leaves her under-trained for her next certificate, destroys her authority with the ratings, and is itself discrimination in employment.
Which Indian statute governs at present? The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, administered by the Directorate General of Shipping.

blocks.p: Four moves: WHY - WHO - WHAT BINDS - WHAT I DO. WHY is limb (a): right, workforce, quality, perspective, retention, commercial, and better standards for everyone. WHO is limb (b): the Organization does programmes - training, associations, fellowships, a World Maritime Day theme, parity built into ordinary programmes; India does policy through the DG Shipping under the 1958 Act - admission, certification, institute approval conditions, training berths, MLC implementation. WHAT BINDS is the MLC table. WHAT I DO is limb (c) in three: the ship, the work, the behaviour.

For limb (c) the three-word cue is CABIN - CRANE - CULTURE: cabin for the physical arrangements and the PPE that fits; crane for work allocated by rank and competence with the right lifting aids; culture for the standard set on day one, the first incident dealt with, and the complaint route that is real.

blocks.p: This is the question on the paper with the weakest available primary evidence, and the answer is built around that rather than pretending otherwise. What is carried at primary grade is the part that matters most - the binding obligations in limb (c) - because MLC 2006 as amended through 2018 was read at source and supplies Article III(d), Article IV, Standard A3.1, Guideline B4.3.1 and Standard A5.1.5. One worked example of an IMO programme with an explicit gender-parity mechanism is also read at source, in the appendix to resolution MEPC.377(80). Everything else in limb (b) is authoritative secondary and is stated at programme and policy level. No IMO resolution number, no Assembly resolution, no DG Shipping circular, rule, notice or scheme number is asserted anywhere in this answer, because MIW holds no licensed text of any such instrument - and a number invented to look authoritative is exactly what fails under an oral follow-up. No statistic is quoted either: no share of the seafaring workforce, no participation figure, no officer-shortfall projection. None can be sourced, and the case in limb (a) is complete without one. Both limits are recorded as open items rather than written around.

notes: LOW TEMPORAL RISK, BECAUSE NOTHING DATE-SENSITIVE IS ASSERTED. The answer relies on the MLC 2006 fundamental rights and Title 3, 4 and 5 provisions, which are stable, and otherwise describes programmes at a level that does not turn on a particular year.

THE MLC EDITION IS THE SAME QUESTION AS Q6 AND IS RESOLVED THE SAME WAY. The operative text at July 2024 is MLC 2006 as amended THROUGH THE 2018 AMENDMENTS. The 2022 amendments do not enter into force until 23 December 2024, five months after this sitting. Guideline B4.3.1's harassment and bullying reference and the Standard A5.1.5 complaint machinery relied on here are both present in the operative 2018 consolidation, read at source; nothing is taken from the later text.

THE INDIAN STATUTE BOUNDARY IS LIVE ON THIS QUESTION AND IS RESOLVED. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the governing statute at this sitting. The MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 2025 COMMENCED 15 MARCH 2026 - twenty months AFTER the sitting - and appears nowhere. The Directorate General of Shipping is named as the administration under the 1958 Act.
THE COASTAL SHIPPING ACT, 2025 is twelve months or more future and appears nowhere. It is recorded because Indian maritime measures are the natural place for a later statute to leak into limb (b).
THE 2025 MLC AMENDMENTS (113th International Labour Conference) are twelve months or more future and are never cited.

THE UN 2030 AGENDA AND ITS GOALS were adopted in 2015 and are operative throughout. The framework is corroborated at source by resolution MEPC.377(80), which recites the 2030 Agenda and cites a numbered Sustainable Development Goal in the same form the stem uses.

THE ONE READ-AT-SOURCE IMO EXAMPLE PRE-DATES THE SITTING. Resolution MEPC.377(80) was adopted 7 July 2023, one year before, and its appendix 2 describes the GHG-SMART programme as running from 2020 to 2025 - operative at the sitting.

questions.understand_first: Strip the policy language away and there are two different things in this question that people constantly run together. One is a proportion - how many of the people on ships are women - and that is a target, something an industry can aim at and may miss for years without anyone breaking a rule. The other is a right - that nobody is kept out of a job, a training place or a promotion because of their sex, and that everybody gets a workplace and a home on board that is safe and decent. The second is already binding on the flag State and therefore on the ship, whatever programmes exist. Once you see that, the last part of the question stops being about attitudes and becomes concrete: the boiler suit that fits, the lockable cabin, the overhaul she is actually trusted with, and what happens the first time somebody says something out of place. The programmes can only get a person to the gangway. What decides whether she is still in the profession in three years happens in the engine room.

blocks.h: 1. The essential difference - what was removed, and what replaced it

blocks.p: The conventional MC engine is mechanically controlled. A chain- or gear-driven camshaft runs the length of the engine and does three jobs: it drives the jerk-type fuel injection pump on each cylinder, it drives the exhaust valve actuator, and it operates the starting air distributor. Every event in the cycle - when injection begins, how long it lasts, when the exhaust valve opens and closes - is written into the geometry of the cams. It is decided at the drawing board and it does not change afterwards. Variable injection timing gives a limited, mechanically produced variation, and reversing is achieved by physically displacing or switching the cam arrangement.

The ME engine is electronically controlled. The camshaft and its drive are removed. In their place there are two things: a supply of high-pressure hydraulic oil, and a computer control system that decides, cycle by cycle and cylinder by cylinder, when and how that oil is released to do the work the cams used to do. The muscle is still hydraulic and mechanical; only the decision has moved from the shape of a cam into software.

That single change is the answer to the whole question, and it is worth stating before the detail. Timing is no longer a property of the engine's geometry; it is a set of values in a control system. Everything else - what the HPS is for, why there is an HCU on each cylinder, what the ELFI or FIVA valve does, and why the fuel pump has become a pressure booster - follows from it.

rows: Camshaft and drive
Camshaft with chain or gear drive, cams for fuel, exhaust valve and starting air distributor

Camshaft eliminated on the fully electronic engine, together with its chain drive and its wear. On some variants the exhaust valve actuation is retained mechanically and only the fuel injection is brought under electronic control
Control
Mechanical and hydraulic; governor and VIT linkage

Engine control system - a main operating panel for the operator, interface units to the bridge and control room, engine control units carrying the governing and safety functions, cylinder control units one per cylinder, and auxiliary control units for the ancillaries
Working medium for actuation
None - the cam does the work directly
High-pressure hydraulic oil from the HPS, the engine's own system oil in the usual arrangement, cleaned to a high standard
Fuel injection
Cam-driven jerk pump; delivery and timing set by cam profile, plunger geometry and helix
Hydraulically driven fuel pressure booster controlled by a servo valve; timing, pressure profile and duration all set electronically
Injection timing
Fixed by cam geometry; limited variation through VIT
Fully variable, continuously, at any load, and independently for each cylinder
Exhaust valve
Cam-driven hydraulic actuator; air spring return
Electronically controlled hydraulic actuation, so opening and closing can be varied with load; air spring return retained
Starting and reversing
Mechanical starting air distributor; reversing by displacing or switching the cam arrangement
Electronically controlled starting air; reversing is a change of control values, giving faster and more repeatable manoeuvring
Cylinder lubrication
Mechanically driven lubricators, feed proportional to speed
Electronically controlled lubricators, feed rate set by load, cylinder oil quality and running condition
Governing
Mechanical or hydraulic governor
Speed control is a function within the control system, with electronic overspeed and safety protection
Running modes
One tuning, fixed
Selectable operating modes - for example a fuel-economy tuning, a low-load tuning for slow steaming, and an emissions-oriented tuning within the engine's certified condition
Part-load behaviour
Injection pressure falls with engine speed, so combustion deteriorates at low load and smoke appears
Injection pressure is independent of engine speed, so full injection pressure is available at low load - smokeless operation to a much lower load
Maintenance
Cam, chain, roller and pump wear; timing adjusted mechanically

Fewer moving parts and no cam or chain wear, but hydraulic oil cleanliness becomes critical, and electronics, sensors, software version control and spare control units become part of the department's work
Diagnostics
Indicator cards and manual measurement
Continuous monitoring of pressures, timings and valve response through the control system, with automatic cylinder balancing

blocks.h: 3. The Hydraulic Power Supply - what it is for

blocks.p: Purpose. The HPS produces and maintains the high-pressure hydraulic oil that is the working medium of the whole engine. It is the muscle that replaced the camshaft. Everything the cams used to drive is now driven by this oil: the fuel pressure boosters, the exhaust valve actuators and, through the control units, the associated functions. It must deliver that pressure steadily, at all loads, and available before the engine is started.
What it consists of. In the usual arrangement:

ul: Engine-driven main hydraulic pumps - variable-displacement axial piston pumps driven from the crankshaft through a step-up gear, which supply the engine once it is running;
Electrically driven start-up and standby pumps, which build up pressure before starting and provide redundancy;
Suction and delivery filtration to a high standard, usually with automatic back-flushing, because the servo valves have very fine clearances and dirt is the principal cause of failure;
Safety and relief valves limiting the maximum pressure, and non-return valves preventing back-flow;
Accumulators smoothing the pressure and providing the instantaneous flow each injection demands;
the high-pressure manifold or rail running along the engine to feed each hydraulic cylinder unit;
pressure, temperature and level instrumentation reporting to the control system, with alarms and slowdown functions.

blocks.p: The working medium is normally the engine's own system lubricating oil, drawn from the main system and given its own additional fine filtration. That is a considerable operational advantage - one oil, one purifier, no separate hydraulic charge - and a considerable operational obligation, because the cleanliness and water content of the system oil now determine whether the engine will run at all.

blocks.h: 4. The Hydraulic Cylinder Unit, and what it contains

blocks.p: What it is. The HCU is the local hydraulic block mounted at each cylinder, at platform level beside the unit. If the HPS is the power station, the HCU is the substation: it takes high-pressure oil from the common supply and distributes it, under the command of that cylinder's own control unit, to the two things that have to be actuated on that cylinder. There is one HCU per cylinder, which is what makes cylinder-by-cylinder control possible.
The components it includes are typically:

ul: the HCU block or base, machined with the internal galleries that distribute the oil - it is the manifold as well as the mounting;
the fuel oil pressure booster, the hydraulically driven intensifier that develops injection pressure - limb (d);
the fuel injection control valve, the ELFI - or, where the combined valve is fitted, the FIVA - limb (c);
the exhaust valve actuator, the hydraulic cylinder that opens the exhaust valve against its air spring;
the exhaust valve control valve, where the exhaust valve is controlled separately from the fuel;
accumulators - one supporting the injection event and one supporting the exhaust valve actuation - which supply the very high instantaneous flow each event needs without collapsing the rail pressure;
filters, non-return valves and safety valves local to the unit;
the high-pressure pipework from the booster to the cylinder cover fuel valves, and the connection to the exhaust valve actuator;
position and pressure sensors reporting booster plunger position, injection pressure and exhaust valve movement back to the cylinder control unit, which is how the system closes the loop;
in many arrangements, the supply to the electronically controlled cylinder lubricator for that unit.

blocks.h: 5. The ELFI and the FIVA valve

blocks.p: Both are fast-acting, electronically controlled proportional servo valves, mounted on the HCU and driven directly by that cylinder's control unit. They are the point at which the electronic decision becomes a hydraulic action - the true replacement for the cam.

rows: ELFI - electronic fuel injection valve

Controls the fuel injection event only. On command from the cylinder control unit it admits high-pressure oil from the HCU accumulator to the underside of the fuel pressure booster's hydraulic piston, and it vents that oil to control the end of injection. Because it is proportional rather than simply open or shut, it controls not just when injection starts and stops but the rate at which oil is admitted - and therefore the shape of the injection pressure profile. Where an ELFI is fitted, the exhaust valve has its own separate control valve
FIVA - fuel injection and valve activation valve

A single proportional valve that performs both functions: it controls the fuel injection event and the exhaust valve actuation from one unit, in one housing, on one command channel. It reduces the component count on the HCU and the number of high-pressure connections, at the cost of concentrating two functions in one item

ul: Both are controlled with position feedback: the valve spool's position is measured and returned to the control unit, which corrects it continuously. That is what makes the timing repeatable rather than merely commanded.

What this buys. Start of injection, injection pressure and rate, duration and end of injection are all set electronically and can be changed at any load. Injection can be shaped - a softer start to reduce peak pressure and NOx, or a sharper one for efficiency. Individual cylinders can be balanced automatically, and a cylinder can be cut out or run at reduced injection without stopping the engine.

The exhaust valve gains the same freedom. Where the valve is electronically controlled, its opening and closing can be varied with load, which changes the effective compression ratio and the scavenging - one of the main reasons an electronically controlled engine burns less fuel across the load range rather than only at its design point.

The constraint that a Chief Engineer must remember is that the settings which the ELFI or FIVA implements are NOx-critical parameters. They may only be varied within the range recorded in the engine's NOx Technical File; a mode or a setting outside that range takes the engine outside its certified condition.

The practical vulnerability is contamination. These valves have very fine clearances and operate at high pressure many times a second. Dirty or wet servo oil sticks them, and a sticking valve shows as an injection timing deviation alarm long before it shows as a broken component - which is why oil cleanliness is the single most important routine on this engine.

blocks.h: 6. The fuel pressure booster compared with the conventional fuel pump

blocks.p: The conventional jerk pump. A cam lifts a plunger inside a barrel. The plunger closes the suction and spill ports and compresses the trapped fuel until it lifts the injector needle. The pressure is generated by the direct mechanical thrust of the cam. Delivery quantity is set by rotating the plunger relative to its helix - by the fuel rack - and timing is set by the cam geometry, with variable injection timing giving limited adjustment. Shutdown is by a puncture valve or by racking to zero. Two consequences follow, and they are the whole of the comparison:

ul: Injection pressure depends on plunger velocity, and plunger velocity depends on engine speed. At low load and low revolutions the pressure falls, atomisation deteriorates, combustion worsens and the engine smokes. That is why a conventional engine has a practical lower limit to clean running.
Timing cannot be changed while running beyond the range the mechanical arrangement allows.

blocks.p: The ME fuel pressure booster. It is a hydraulically driven pressure intensifier, not a pump in the jerk sense. Low-pressure fuel from the ship's fuel supply system fills the fuel side of the booster. On command, the ELFI or FIVA valve admits high-pressure servo oil to a hydraulic piston of large area, rigidly connected to a fuel plunger of much smaller area. The pressure on the fuel side is multiplied in proportion to the ratio of the two areas, and rises to injection pressure. When the control valve vents the servo oil, the pressure collapses, injection ends cleanly, and a spring returns the assembly ready for the next cycle.

blocks.p: What the change buys, in operating terms. Full injection pressure at low load means clean combustion far down the load range, which is what makes genuine slow steaming possible without smoke, fouled turbochargers and unburnt fuel in the exhaust. Variable timing and rate shaping allow the engine to be tuned across the load range rather than at one design point, improving consumption at part load and giving a lever on NOx formation. Cylinder-by-cylinder control allows automatic balancing and much simpler management of a defective unit.

What it costs. A dependence on hydraulic oil cleanliness and dryness that has no equivalent on an MC engine; the need for electrical power and a working control system before the engine will start at all, with the redundancy that implies; a department that must be competent in electronics, sensors and software version control as well as in mechanics; and the discipline that the injection settings are NOx-critical parameters and may only be varied within the range recorded in the engine's NOx Technical File.

Four short notes at four marks each. The written-answer discipline is equal time, and the risk here is different from the usual one: limb (a) invites a very long list, and a candidate who writes fifteen differences has spent eight marks' worth of time earning four. Six to eight well-chosen differences in a table is enough; the marks in limbs (b), (c) and (d) are waiting.

Limb (b) is really two questions - the purpose of the HPS, and what the HCU is and contains - so split it deliberately. Limb (d) says 'describe the differences', which means a comparison, not a description of the booster alone. A table earns more than prose in both.

blocks.h: The one sentence that carries the whole question

blocks.p: The camshaft did not become unnecessary; it became software. The work is still done hydraulically and mechanically - oil at high pressure still pushes a piston that still pushes a plunger - but the decision about when and how fast has moved out of the shape of a cam and into a control system. Say that once and every limb follows: the HPS is the muscle that replaced the cam, the HCU is where that muscle is applied at each cylinder, the ELFI or FIVA is the point at which the electronic decision becomes a hydraulic action, and the booster is the actuator that used to be a cam-driven pump.

ul: Calling the ME engine's fuel pump a jerk pump. It is a hydraulically driven pressure intensifier; the pressure comes from an area ratio, not from a cam.
Saying the ME engine is 'electric'. Only the control is electronic; the power is hydraulic and mechanical throughout.
Forgetting that the servo oil is normally the engine's own system oil, and that its cleanliness therefore becomes a running requirement rather than a housekeeping preference.
Confusing ELFI and FIVA. ELFI is fuel only; FIVA does fuel and exhaust valve in one valve. If you can only remember one thing about limb (c), remember that.

Saying the camshaft is eliminated on every variant. On some, the exhaust valve actuation remains mechanically driven and only the injection is electronic - say that variants differ rather than overstating.
Listing advantages without the operational costs. Oil cleanliness, electrical dependence, control-system redundancy and the new competencies are half the answer.
Quoting a hydraulic pressure, injection pressure or consumption gain. These are builder- and variant-specific; an unsourced figure invites the one question you cannot answer.

'Where does the hydraulic oil come from?' The engine's own system lubricating oil in the usual arrangement, given additional fine filtration - which is why water in the system oil is an engine-stopping problem, not just a lubrication problem.
'Why are there accumulators on the HCU?' Because an injection event demands a very large flow for a very short time, and without local storage the rail pressure would collapse.
'Why can an ME engine slow steam cleanly?' Because injection pressure is independent of engine speed - the booster is driven by servo oil at full pressure whatever the revolutions.

'What must you check before changing an engine running mode?' That the settings remain within the ranges recorded in the engine's NOx Technical File. Modes and timings are NOx-critical parameters. This is the answer that links limb (c) to a regulatory obligation and it is worth a mark on its own.

'How do you start an ME engine after a blackout?' The electrically driven start-up hydraulic pumps must build up pressure and the control system must be alive before the engine can be started - it is not simply a matter of air on the turning gear side.
'What is the commonest cause of servo valve trouble?' Contamination - dirt or water in the servo oil - showing first as a timing deviation alarm.
What three things did the camshaft do on an MC engine? Drove the fuel pump, the exhaust valve actuator and the starting air distributor.
How does the booster generate injection pressure? A large-area hydraulic piston acts on a small-area fuel plunger; the pressure rises in the ratio of the areas.
What ends injection on an ME engine? Venting the servo oil through the control valve - a clean cut-off.

Name five components on an HCU. The block itself, the fuel pressure booster, the ELFI or FIVA valve, the exhaust valve actuator, and the accumulators - plus local filters, safety valves and position sensors.
How is an ME engine reversed? By changing the control values - injection and exhaust valve timing are re-set electronically; there is no cam to shift.

What new competencies does the ME engine demand of your department? Hydraulic cleanliness discipline, sensor and electronics fault-finding, software version control, and the management of control-unit spares.

blocks.p: The whole question is one chain, and if you can draw the chain you can answer all four limbs: HPS - rail - HCU - ELFI or FIVA - booster - injector, with the cylinder control unit sitting above the ELFI or FIVA sending the command and receiving the feedback. Limb (b) is the first three links, limb (c) is the fourth, limb (d) is the fifth, and limb (a) is what the chain replaced.

For limb (a), six differences in one line: no camshaft, electronic control, hydraulic actuation, variable timing, software reversing, and pressure independent of speed. Then add the maintenance trade - fewer moving parts but oil cleanliness and electronics.

blocks.p: This question carries no statutory content and there is no primary instrument to read; the whole of it is engineering, reasoned from mechanical and hydraulic first principles and from standard shipboard practice. Three limits are declared rather than concealed. First, no engine builder documentation is held in the MIW corpus in any form - no project guide, no operating manual, no service letter - so nothing is quoted or attributed to one. Second, and following from that, no quantity is asserted anywhere on this question: no hydraulic system pressure, no injection pressure, no filtration rating, no part-load consumption gain and no minimum stable load. Each is builder- and variant-specific, and the protocol requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision - so the mechanisms are described qualitatively and completely, which is what the stem asks and what earns the marks. Third, engine variants genuinely differ, most importantly in whether the exhaust valve actuation remains mechanically driven or is brought under electronic control; the answer says the variants differ rather than presenting one arrangement as universal. The one regulatory statement made - that the injection settings are NOx-critical parameters constrained by the engine's NOx Technical File - rests on MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13.8, which was read at source for this paper's Q9.

quick_revision.recall_15s: The camshaft became software. MC: cam drives fuel pump, exhaust valve actuator and starting air distributor; timing fixed by cam geometry; injection pressure falls with speed. ME: camshaft removed, replaced by high-pressure servo oil plus a control system - main operating panel, engine and cylinder control units. HPS makes and maintains the servo oil: engine-driven and electric pumps, fine automatic filtration, safety and non-return valves, accumulators, rail, instrumentation - normally the engine's own system oil. HCU is the block at each cylinder: booster, ELFI or FIVA, exhaust valve actuator, accumulators, filters, sensors. ELFI does fuel only; FIVA does fuel and exhaust valve. Booster is an intensifier - big hydraulic piston on a small fuel plunger, pressure by area ratio, independent of engine speed, so clean combustion far down the load range. Settings are NOx-critical and bounded by the NOx Technical File.
critical_numbers: One HCU per cylinder - which is what makes cylinder-by-cylinder control possible
The camshaft did three jobs on an MC engine: fuel pump, exhaust valve actuator, starting air distributor
ELFI controls one function; FIVA controls two
NO pressure, filtration rating, consumption gain or minimum load figure is quoted - all are builder- and variant-specific
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None governs the engine architecture. The one regulatory constraint that matters in the engine room is MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13.8: the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 applies to certification, testing and measurement, which is why the injection settings the ELFI or FIVA implements may only be varied within the range recorded in the engine's NOx Technical File.
quick_revision.major_trap: Calling the ME fuel pressure booster a jerk pump, or saying the pressure comes from a cam. It is a hydraulic intensifier and the pressure comes from the ratio of the hydraulic piston area to the fuel plunger area, which is why injection pressure is independent of engine speed. The second trap is treating ELFI and FIVA as the same thing: ELFI controls fuel only, FIVA controls fuel and the exhaust valve.

questions.memory_cue: One chain, and each link is a route step: HPS (3) - rail - HCU (4) - ELFI or FIVA (5) - booster (6) - injector. Limb (a) at step (2) is what the chain replaced, and step (1) is why it was replaced.
questions.understand_first: On the older engine a single long shaft with lumps on it decided everything. The shape of each lump decided when fuel went in, how long for, and when the exhaust valve opened - and once the shaft was made, those decisions were fixed for the life of the engine. That was fine at the load the engine was designed for and poor everywhere else, which is why the old engine smokes when you slow her down: the pump is driven by the shaft, so as the engine turns more slowly the fuel is squeezed more slowly and sprayed more coarsely. The newer engine keeps all the muscle and throws away the shaft. Oil at very high pressure is kept ready in a common supply, and at each cylinder a small fast electrically-commanded valve decides the instant it is let through and how quickly. That oil pushes a large piston which pushes a small plunger, and because the small end is much smaller than the big end the fuel comes out at very high pressure - regardless of how slowly the engine happens to be turning. The engine can now be re-timed by changing numbers instead of changing metal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the ME versus MC engine question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The essential difference - the camshaft became software. 2 The differences in detail. 3 The HPS and its purpose. 4 The HCU and its components. 5 ELFI and FIVA. 6 The fuel pressure booster compared with the jerk pump.
retrieval_cards.why: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. Limb (a) is section 2 and must not be allowed to eat the other three limbs' time; limb (b) is two questions and needs both sections 3 and 4.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the camshaft do on an MC engine, and what replaced it on an ME engine?
retrieval_cards.answer: It drove the jerk-type fuel injection pump, the exhaust valve actuator and the starting air distributor, and its cam geometry fixed all the timing. On the ME engine it is replaced by two things: a high-pressure hydraulic supply that does the physical work, and an electronic control system that decides when and how fast that work is done - cycle by cycle and cylinder by cylinder.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the architectural answer, and every other limb follows from it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the purpose of the HPS, and what does it consist of?
retrieval_cards.answer: To produce and maintain the high-pressure hydraulic oil that is the engine's working medium, steadily at all loads and available before starting. It comprises engine-driven main hydraulic pumps, electrically driven start-up and standby pumps, fine automatic filtration, safety and non-return valves, accumulators, the high-pressure rail to each HCU, and instrumentation reporting to the control system. The medium is normally the engine's own system lubricating oil, given additional fine filtration.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for the purpose, so state it as a purpose first and then list the hardware.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the HCU and which components does it include?
retrieval_cards.answer: The local hydraulic block mounted at each cylinder - one per cylinder - which distributes high-pressure oil under that cylinder's control unit. It carries the HCU block with its internal galleries, the fuel oil pressure booster, the ELFI or FIVA valve, the exhaust valve actuator and its control valve where separate, accumulators for injection and for the exhaust valve, local filters, non-return and safety valves, the high-pressure pipework to the fuel valves, and position and pressure sensors feeding back to the cylinder control unit.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'which components are included', so a genuine list is the mark - and one-per-cylinder is why per-cylinder control exists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an ELFI valve and a FIVA valve?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both are fast-acting electronically controlled proportional servo valves on the HCU, driven by the cylinder control unit with position feedback. The ELFI controls the fuel injection event only, and the exhaust valve then has its own separate control valve. The FIVA is a single valve that controls both the fuel injection and the exhaust valve actuation, reducing the component count at the cost of concentrating two functions in one item.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem writes them as ELFI/FIVA as though they were one thing; distinguishing them is the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an ME fuel pressure booster generate injection pressure?
retrieval_cards.answer: Low-pressure fuel from the supply system fills the fuel side. On command, the ELFI or FIVA valve admits high-pressure servo oil to a large-area hydraulic piston rigidly connected to a much smaller-area fuel plunger. The fuel pressure rises in proportion to the ratio of the two areas until the injector opens. Venting the servo oil collapses the pressure and ends injection cleanly, and a spring returns the assembly.
retrieval_cards.why: Area ratio, not cam thrust, is the whole of limb (d).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can an ME engine slow steam cleanly when an MC engine cannot?
retrieval_cards.answer: On a jerk pump the injection pressure depends on plunger velocity, which depends on engine speed, so at low revolutions the pressure falls, atomisation deteriorates and the engine smokes. On the ME engine the booster is driven by servo oil at full system pressure whatever the engine speed, so full injection pressure and good atomisation are available far down the load range.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single most useful operational consequence of the whole redesign.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What regulatory constraint applies to the injection settings the ELFI or FIVA implements?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are NOx-critical parameters. Under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13.8 the revised NOx Technical Code applies to certification, testing and measurement, and the engine's NOx Technical File records the components, settings and permitted adjustment ranges. A running mode or a setting outside the recorded range takes the engine outside its certified condition.
retrieval_cards.why: It links the engine's flexibility to a legal boundary, and it is the answer that turns a technical description into a management-level one.

blocks.h: 1. What IMO is, and the organs that do the work

blocks.p: The International Maritime Organization is the specialised agency of the United Nations responsible for the safety and security of shipping and for the prevention of pollution from ships. It works through a two-tier governing structure - an Assembly and a Council - together with five main committees supported by seven sub-committees, all served by a permanent Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General. The governing organs decide policy, budget and membership questions; the technical output that actually reaches a ship comes almost entirely from the committees.

ul: The highest governing body. All Member States sit in it, each with one vote, and Associate Members participate without the full voting rights of Members.
Meets in regular session once every two years. An extraordinary session may be convened between regular sessions where the business requires it.

Approves the work programme and votes the budget, and determines the financial arrangements of the Organization. Nothing the committees plan can proceed unless the Assembly has funded and programmed it.
Elects the Council for the following two-year term.
Receives and considers the reports of the Council and of the committees, and decides what action to take on their recommendations.

Adopts Assembly resolutions - recommendations to Governments, guidelines, and codes - under Article 15(j) of the Convention on the IMO. This is the function the Assembly reserves to itself and does not delegate to the Council.

Worked example read at source: the 2011 ESP Code was adopted by the Assembly as resolution A.1049(27) on 30 November 2011, expressly under Article 15(j) and on the recommendation of the Maritime Safety Committee at its 89th session. That single recital shows the whole machine working - technical body proposes, governing body adopts.

40 Members, elected by the Assembly for a two-year term in three categories: (a) ten States with the largest interest in providing international shipping services; (b) ten States with the largest interest in international seaborne trade; (c) twenty States elected to secure representation of all major geographic areas. The three categories exist so that the organ cannot be captured by tonnage alone.

Between Assembly sessions it performs all the functions of the Assembly, except the function of making recommendations to Governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention, which the Assembly keeps to itself. That single exception is what stops the executive organ from legislating in the governing organ's absence.
Supervises the work of the Organization and co-ordinates the activities of its organs, and receives the committees' reports between Assembly sessions.
Considers the draft work programme and budget prepared by the Secretary-General and submits them to the Assembly with its own comments and recommendations.
Appoints the Secretary-General, subject to Assembly approval, and takes responsibility for the arrangements for the Secretariat.
Concludes agreements and arrangements with other organizations, subject to Assembly approval.

Position at this sitting: the serving Council was elected at the 33rd Assembly in December 2023 for the 2024-2025 biennium and is in the first year of that term. The amendment that would enlarge the Council to 52 Members was adopted in December 2021 but requires acceptance by two thirds of Members and is not in force; the correct figure is therefore 40.

blocks.h: 4. The five main committees and what each owns

rows: Maritime Safety Committee (MSC)
The highest technical body: navigational safety, construction and equipment, manning from a safety standpoint, casualty investigation, salvage and rescue
Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC)
Prevention and control of pollution from ships - MARPOL and its amendments, ballast water, anti-fouling and greenhouse-gas measures
Legal Committee
Any legal matter within the scope of the Organization, liability and compensation conventions in particular
Technical Cooperation Committee
Implementation of the Organization's technical assistance work, particularly for developing States
Facilitation Committee
Elimination of unnecessary formalities and red tape in international shipping - the FAL Convention

blocks.p: All five are open to all Member States and each reports to the Assembly through the Council. The point that matters for a ship is that MSC and MEPC are the two that adopt amendments to the mandatory instruments - SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Lines, STCW, the mandatory codes - and they do so by resolution, under the amendment article of the convention concerned. The Assembly does not adopt SOLAS or MARPOL amendments; the relevant committee does. Adoption is followed by the tacit acceptance procedure: the amendment is deemed accepted on a stated date unless a stated proportion of Parties objects, and enters into force on a further stated date. That is why a ship can be bound by a change no national parliament ever debated.

blocks.h: 5. The seven sub-committees and the role they perform

blocks.p: The sub-committees are HTW (Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping), III (Implementation of IMO Instruments), NCSR (Navigation, Communications and Search and Rescue), PPR (Pollution Prevention and Response), SDC (Ship Design and Construction), SSE (Ship Systems and Equipment) and CCC (Carriage of Cargoes and Containers).

Their role is preparatory and technical. A committee sits for about a week and cannot itself draft detailed regulation, so it remits the work to the sub-committee holding the relevant expertise. The sub-committee develops the draft text, guidelines or unified interpretation, settles the technical argument, and reports back to its parent committee - MSC, MEPC, or both, since several sub-committees serve two parents. The typical life of a work item is therefore: a Member State or organization submits a proposal; the committee accepts it into the work programme; the sub-committee develops the text over one or more sessions, often through a correspondence group between sessions; the committee approves the draft and circulates it; and the committee then adopts it by resolution at a later session.

A sub-committee adopts nothing. It prepares, the parent committee approves, and the committee or the Assembly adopts. That division is what keeps technical depth and treaty-making authority in different hands, and it is also why the sub-committee stage is where a shipowner's or a class society's technical argument is actually won or lost - by the time the committee adopts, the engineering has been settled.

A convention is a formal, legally binding treaty between States. It is negotiated and adopted at a diplomatic conference convened for the purpose, or by the Assembly, and is then opened for signature, ratification, acceptance, approval or accession. Signature alone does not bind: the State becomes a Contracting Government only when it deposits its instrument with the Secretary-General as depositary.

A convention enters into force only when the conditions written into the convention itself are satisfied - typically a stated number of Contracting States whose combined merchant fleets represent a stated percentage of world gross tonnage, followed by a stated waiting period. It then binds only those States that have become party to it, and it reaches a ship through the flag State's own national law. Its detailed content is normally kept current not by re-negotiation but by amendment under its own amendment article, using tacit acceptance. Example: the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, whose amendments are adopted by MSC under article VIII.

blocks.h: 7. Protocol, Code and Resolution - how each differs, with examples

rows: Protocol
A separate treaty instrument that amends, supplements or modifies a parent convention, used where the change is too large for the ordinary amendment procedure. A State may have to be party to both
MARPOL Annex VI defines itself as the Annex to the 1973 Convention as modified by the Protocol of 1978 and the Protocol of 1997
Code
A detailed technical instrument. Of itself it is recommendatory; it becomes mandatory only when a convention makes it so. Mandatory status is a property of the route, not of the word 'Code'
SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 makes parts 1 and 2 of the RO Code mandatory and part 3 recommendatory - one Code, both statuses. Regulation XI-1/2 makes the 2011 ESP Code mandatory
Resolution
The formal decision of the Assembly or of a committee. It is the vehicle by which an instrument is adopted or guidance issued, and is recommendatory unless what it carries has been made mandatory
A.1049(27) adopting the ESP Code; MEPC.377(80), which carries a strategy and creates no obligation; MEPC.385(81), which adopts mandatory MARPOL amendments

blocks.p: The three examples in the last row make the point that no single label settles the question. Two resolutions of the same committee, adopted eight months apart, do entirely different legal work: MEPC.377(80) carries a strategy and obliges no ship to do anything, while MEPC.385(81) adopts amendments to MARPOL Annex VI which, once in force, bind every Party. The label 'MEPC resolution' tells you nothing; the route does.

Adoption is not entry into force. MEPC.385(81) was adopted on 22 March 2024, four months before this sitting, and is still not binding on anyone: it is deemed accepted on 1 February 2025 and enters into force on 1 August 2025. The same distinction runs through the whole hierarchy, and it is the distinction the examiner is most likely to probe in the oral. Alongside these four instruments sit the non-binding working papers of the system - circulars, guidelines and unified interpretations (MSC.1/Circ., MEPC.1/Circ., MSC-MEPC. joint circulars). They explain how a requirement is to be applied and are heavily used at survey, but they create no obligation of their own unless a convention pulls them in by reference.

The marks in limb (a) sit in the function column, not in the names. Anyone can write 'MSC, MEPC, Legal, TC, FAL'; the mark comes from saying what each one is for. The examiner has also asked one narrow question inside limb (a) - what role the sub-committees play in supporting the main committees - and it is the part most candidates leave out. Step 5 answers it explicitly and states the negative as well as the positive: a sub-committee has no adoption power.

Limb (b) carries the same eight marks and is far quicker to write, so write it properly. A three-column table with a worked example in every row banks the marks in about a third of the time limb (a) takes.

blocks.h: The one idea that makes limb (b) easy

blocks.p: Candidates try to memorise which instruments are 'mandatory'. That model does not survive a follow-up question. The right model is: obligation comes from the treaty route, not from the label. The RO Code is the cleanest proof available - SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 makes parts 1 and 2 of that single Code mandatory and part 3 recommendatory. Same document, same title, two different legal statuses, decided entirely by what the Convention says about each part.

blocks.h: How a change actually reaches your ship

blocks.p: This is the thread that ties both limbs together and it is worth being able to state in the oral. A Member State submits a proposal to a committee. The committee accepts it into the work programme and remits the technical work to the sub-committee that holds the expertise. The sub-committee drafts, argues and reports back. The committee approves the draft and circulates it to Parties. At a later session the committee adopts it by resolution under the convention's amendment article. Tacit acceptance then runs: the amendment is deemed accepted on a stated date unless enough Parties object, and enters into force on a further stated date. The flag State gives it domestic effect, the certificate changes, and a surveyor arrives to verify it.

MEPC.385(81) is that sequence caught in the middle. It has been adopted; it has not been deemed accepted; it is not in force. Anyone who can walk an examiner along that chain has both limbs of this question, because limb (a) is the machinery and limb (b) is the instruments the machinery produces.

ul: Naming only MSC and MEPC as the 'main committees'. There are five, and the question says 'various main committees'.
Saying the Assembly meets annually. It meets in regular session every two years.
Describing the sub-committees as if they adopt regulation. They do not.
Writing that a Code is 'always mandatory' or 'always recommendatory'. Neither is true.
Confusing a Protocol with an amendment. An ordinary amendment is adopted under the convention's own amendment article; a Protocol is a separate treaty.
Giving no examples in limb (b) when the question expressly asks for at least one of each. That is a straight loss of marks for something the candidate already knows.

The Council's size. An amendment enlarging the Council from 40 to 52 was adopted in December 2021 but requires acceptance by two thirds of Members and was not in force at this sitting. Write 40; if the enlargement is mentioned, mention it as an amendment not yet in force.

Adopted is not in force. MEPC.385(81) was adopted at MEPC 81 in March 2024, four months before this paper, and still enters into force only on 1 August 2025. A script that calls it 'the current requirement' is wrong at this sitting.
The Secretary-General. Arsenio Dominguez took office on 1 January 2024, six months before this paper.
Being asked in the oral 'so is the ISM Code a convention?' No - it is a Code given mandatory force by SOLAS chapter IX.
Being asked which organ adopts MARPOL amendments. MEPC does, by resolution, under MARPOL article 16 - not the Assembly.
Which committee would deal with a new requirement for lifeboat release gear? MSC, remitted to SSE.
Who adopted the 2011 ESP Code, and on whose recommendation? The Assembly, by A.1049(27), on the recommendation of MSC 89.
What is the difference between adoption and entry into force? Adoption is the decision to make the text; entry into force is when it starts to bind, on the conditions the instrument itself sets.
Name a Code that is only partly mandatory. The RO Code - parts 1 and 2 mandatory, part 3 recommendatory, under SOLAS XI-1/1.
Who appoints the Secretary-General? The Council, subject to Assembly approval.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is top down: Assembly (everyone, every two years) - Council (40, executive) - Committees (five, technical) - Sub-committees (seven, preparatory) - Secretariat. For the five committees use two engines and three others: MSC and MEPC do the mandatory work; Legal, TC and FAL do the rest. For limb (b), one sentence: a Convention binds, a Protocol changes what binds, a Code supplies the detail, a Resolution is how the decision was taken.

Recited in resolution A.1049(27), read at source this session
MEPC's functions under Article 38
Recited in MEPC.377(80) and MEPC.385(81), both read at source

The Organization's published account of its structure - authoritative secondary
Five committees, seven sub-committees
The Organization's published account of its structure

blocks.p: The organs, their functions and the committee and sub-committee lists are stable and were confirmed for this sitting. Two items are genuinely date-sensitive. The first is the Council's size: the enlargement to 52 had been adopted but had not entered into force at July 2024, and a candidate answering a later sitting must re-check that position rather than reuse this figure. The second is the standing of MEPC.385(81), which is correct as 'adopted, not in force' only for a sitting before 1 August 2025. The Secretary-General's identity is likewise sitting-specific. No copy of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization is held in the corpus, so the composition and meeting-cycle facts in limb (a) rest on the Organization's own published account - authoritative secondary, and recorded as such rather than presented as a treaty reading.

notes: EXACT DONOR, FORWARD DIRECTION - THE INVERTED CASE. QP2402-Q1 (February 2024) is five months EARLIER than this sitting. Forward contamination from the donor is therefore impossible; the class that can fire is an earlier donor MISSING something that arrived in the window. The February-to-July 2024 window was searched and four candidates were examined.

WINDOW ITEM 1 - MEPC 81 (18-22 March 2024) fell between the donor and this paper. It changes nothing about the Organization's organs. It did adopt MEPC.385(81), which is used in this answer precisely BECAUSE it is adopted and not in force - it is the sitting's own live illustration of the adoption / entry-into-force distinction.
WINDOW ITEM 2 - MSC 108 (May 2024) also fell in the window. No change to the committee or sub-committee structure.

WINDOW ITEM 3 - the SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024 became the operative edition on 1 JULY 2024, when MSC.521(106) entered into force. That boundary is decisive for Q5; for this question it changes nothing of substance, but it is the reason SOLAS chapter XI-1 is cited here from the 2024 edition rather than the previous one.
WINDOW ITEM 4 - no amendment to the Convention on the IMO entered into force in the window.

COUNCIL SIZE - RE-CHECKED, NOT INHERITED. Resolution A.1152(32), adopted December 2021, would enlarge the Council from 40 to 52 Members. It amends the Convention on the IMO and requires acceptance by two thirds of Members. NOT IN FORCE at July 2024. The answer states 40 and flags the amendment B_CURRENCY_CHECK.

THE COUNCIL'S BIENNIUM. The Council serving was elected at the 33rd Assembly in December 2023 for the 2024-2025 biennium, so at this sitting it is in the FIRST year of that biennium. The donor's sentence about the Council was re-authored rather than copied.

OFFICE HOLDER. The Secretary-General took office 1 January 2024. The donor described that as a change 'seven weeks before this sitting'; at July 2024 that sentence is false as written, so this answer states six months instead. Not corpus-verified; recorded as authoritative secondary.

ASSEMBLY CYCLE. The 33rd Assembly (resolutions adopted 6 December 2023) is the operative cycle. The 34th Assembly adopted on 3 December 2025, seventeen months AFTER this sitting - no A.12xx(34) resolution may appear, and none does.

EXAMPLES CHECKED FOR CURRENCY. A.1049(27) (November 2011), MSC.349(92) RO Code, the 1978 and 1997 MARPOL Protocols and MEPC.377(80) (July 2023) all pre-date the sitting and were in force or operative at it. MEPC.385(81) pre-dates the sitting as an ADOPTION only and is described as such. No example used here is a post-sitting import.

CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE LATER ALTERNATE. QP2502-Q1 (February 2025) was read as a control. Every statement it carries that this answer does not is either identical in substance or is a February 2025 sitting-relative sentence; nothing in it was imported.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two separate tasks. (a) Describe the Organization itself - its organs, what each does, and specifically what the sub-committees contribute to the main committees. (b) A pure instrument-hierarchy question: define a convention, then distinguish Protocol, Code and Resolution from it and from each other, each with an example. Limb (b) is definitional and is marked as heavily as limb (a).
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8, printed against each limb. The candidate who spends twelve marks' worth of writing on the IMO organs and four lines on the instrument types loses half of limb (b).
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can name the organs correctly and, more importantly, can say what each ACTUALLY DOES rather than listing acronyms; and that the candidate understands that 'mandatory' is not a property of the instrument type but of the route by which it was made binding.

The donor QP2402-Q1 read in full, and the later alternate QP2502-Q1 read as a control only

questions.understand_first: This question is not testing whether you can list acronyms. retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a Code mandatory?

retrieval_cards.why: Obligation follows the treaty route, not the label. This is the conceptual mark in limb (b).
