QP2407 Q3 - MEPC, and the resolutions by which it acts

blocks.h: 1. Which instrument is 'the revised strategy', and what it replaced

blocks.p: The revised strategy is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, adopted by the Marine Environment Protection Committee as resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80. It replaces the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018, resolution MEPC.304(72), which the 2023 resolution expressly revokes as from the date of adoption. The Committee agreed at the same time to keep the Strategy under review with a view to adopting a further revised strategy in 2028.

The Strategy is a policy instrument, not a regulation. It binds no ship directly. Obligation arrives only when a measure it calls for is adopted as an amendment to MARPOL Annex VI and enters into force. Saying that clearly is the first mark on this question, because it explains why the short-term measures already bite and the mid-term measures do not.

The Strategy sets out the scale of the problem in its own words: the Third IMO GHG Study 2014 estimated international shipping at some 2.2% of anthropogenic CO2 in 2012, and the Fourth IMO GHG Study 2020 at some 2.89% of global anthropogenic GHG in 2018, with emissions potentially reaching 90% to 130% of 2008 levels by 2050 if nothing is done.

Vision. IMO remains committed to reducing GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of urgency, aims to phase them out as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition.
Objectives. The Strategy states three:

ol: to enhance IMO's contribution to global efforts by addressing GHG emissions from international shipping - expressly linked to the Paris Agreement and to the UN 2030 Agenda and its SDG 13, urgent action to combat climate change;
to identify actions to be implemented by the shipping sector, while addressing impacts on States and recognising shipping's role in global trade;
to identify actions and measures to help achieve those objectives, including incentives for research and development and the monitoring of emissions.

blocks.p: The Strategy sets four levels of ambition, and they are the heart of the answer:

rows: Carbon intensity of the ship
To decline through further improvement of the energy efficiency of new ships - the Strategy commits to a review with the aim of strengthening the energy efficiency design requirements
Carbon intensity of international shipping
To decline: reduce CO2 emissions per transport work, as an average across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030 compared to 2008
Uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and/or energy sources
To increase, to represent at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030
GHG emissions from international shipping to reach net zero

To peak emissions as soon as possible and reach net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, taking into account different national circumstances, while pursuing efforts towards phasing them out

blocks.p: Two points about how these are written repay attention. The 2050 ambition is net-zero GHG, not carbon-neutral CO2, and it is expressed as by or around 2050 rather than as a hard date - the qualification was the price of consensus and it is part of the text. And the whole set is to be read on a well-to-wake basis, taking into account the life cycle GHG intensity of marine fuels under the LCA guidelines (MEPC.376(80)), so that emissions are not simply shifted out of the ship's funnel and into the fuel's production chain.
Distinct from the levels of ambition, and often confused with them, are the two indicative checkpoints on the way to net zero. They are expressed as total annual GHG emissions, not as intensity:

ul: reduce total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, compared to 2008; and
reduce total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, compared to 2008.

blocks.p: The distinction is a real examination point. An intensity target can be met while total emissions rise, if the fleet and the trade grow; an absolute checkpoint cannot. The 2023 Strategy is the first IMO instrument to set absolute reduction figures at all, and that - more than any single percentage - is what makes it a step change from the 2018 Initial Strategy.

ul: The principles already enshrined in existing instruments: non-discrimination and no more favourable treatment, from MARPOL and the other IMO conventions; and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances, from the UNFCCC, its Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
The requirement that all ships give full and complete effect, regardless of flag, to mandatory measures implementing the Strategy.
The need to consider the impacts of measures on States, particularly least developed countries and small island developing States.
The need for evidence-based decision-making balanced with the precautionary approach.

blocks.p: The first two principles pull against each other, and knowing that is worth a mark. No more favourable treatment means a measure must apply to every ship on the same terms whatever her flag; common but differentiated responsibilities means States are not equally placed to bear the cost. Reconciling the two is the reason the mid-term measures carry a comprehensive impact assessment and a revenue-disbursement argument, rather than being simply drafted and adopted.

blocks.h: 6. Short-term measures - and where they stand at this sitting

blocks.p: The Strategy defines short-term measures as those finalized and agreed by the Committee between 2018 and 2023. They are already in MARPOL Annex VI and they are the measures a ship is actually complying with today:

ul: the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) and the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP), introduced by MEPC.203(62);
the IMO Data Collection System (DCS) for fuel oil consumption, introduced by MEPC.278(70) for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above;

the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI), the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) with its A to E rating, and the enhanced SEEMP including Part III, all introduced by MEPC.328(76), the 2021 revised Annex VI.

blocks.p: The Strategy also fixes a deadline for looking at them again: under regulations 25.3 and 28.11 of MARPOL Annex VI, the review of the mandatory goal-based technical and operational measures shall be completed by 1 January 2026. At this sitting that review is running and has not reported.

blocks.h: 7. The basket of candidate mid-term measures

blocks.p: The Strategy requires a basket of candidate mid-term measures to be finalized and agreed by the Committee by 2025, comprising both of the following, together:

rows: Technical element

A goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the marine fuel's GHG intensity - a limit on how much GHG each unit of energy used on board may carry, tightening over time, measured well-to-wake
Economic element

A measure on the basis of a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism - putting a price on the emissions, with the candidate designs to be assessed against specific criteria in the comprehensive impact assessment

blocks.p: Beyond the basket, the Strategy lists other candidate mid-term measures that may be finalized between 2023 and 2030: annual IMO GHG emission and carbon intensity estimates from the DCS; a feedback mechanism on implementation; further development of the LCA guidelines; a regulatory assessment of the safety aspects of reducing GHG emissions and a road map to support safe delivery; measures addressing methane and nitrous oxide and further work on volatile organic compounds; incentives for first movers; and measures encouraging port developments including onshore power supply from renewable sources. Potential synergies with the existing CII are expressly to be considered.

Where this stands at this sitting is the point on which the answer must be exact. The Strategy's own follow-up timetable sets approval of the measures at MEPC 83 in spring 2025, adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session about six months after MEPC 83, and entry into force sixteen months after adoption, in 2027. In July 2024 the basket has therefore been neither approved nor adopted, and no mid-term measure is in force. It is a programme of work with dates attached, and it must be described as one.

blocks.h: 8. Long-term measures, the timetable and the review

ul: Long-term measures are defined as measures finalized and agreed by the Committee beyond 2030, to be developed as part of the 2028 review of the Strategy. The Strategy deliberately does not specify them; that is the honest answer to the 'long-term goals' part of the question, and inventing content for it is a way to lose marks.

The follow-up timetable runs: MEPC 80 (2023) initiation of the comprehensive impact assessment and Phase III of the work plan; MEPC 81 (spring 2024) interim report and finalization of the basket; MEPC 82 (autumn 2024) finalized impact-assessment report; MEPC 83 (spring 2025) approval of measures; an extraordinary session about six months later for adoption; entry into force sixteen months after that.

The impacts of any measure on States are to be assessed and taken into account before adoption, against eight criteria: geographic remoteness and connectivity to main markets, cargo value and type, transport dependency, transport costs, food security, disaster response, cost-effectiveness, and socio-economic progress and development.

The Strategy is subject to a five-yearly review, the first due in 2028, taking account of updated emission estimates, reduction options, IPCC reports and data on the impacts of measures already applied.

blocks.h: 9. The potential impact on the maritime industry

rows: Fuels

A well-to-wake fuel intensity standard makes the production pathway part of compliance. LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and biofuels are each judged on life-cycle intensity rather than on funnel CO2, and a fuel that looks clean on board may not qualify
Newbuilding and design

Dual-fuel and fuel-flexible machinery, larger and differently shaped fuel tanks, and reserved space for future retrofit. Asset life of twenty-five years against a 2050 net-zero ambition makes every ship ordered now a decision about the 2040s
Existing tonnage

EEXI and CII already bite. Engine power limitation, hull and propeller efficiency work, air lubrication, wind assistance and speed management become commercial decisions, and a poor CII rating requires a corrective action plan
Operating cost
An emissions pricing mechanism, when it arrives, converts fuel consumption into a second, separate cost line - and it will be paid by whoever the contract says pays it
Chartering and contracts
Charterparties must allocate the cost and the rating consequence of the charterer's speed and routeing instructions. Emissions clauses become as normal as bunker clauses
Safety and the human element
Ammonia is toxic, hydrogen and methanol are low-flashpoint. The Strategy itself calls for a regulatory assessment of safety aspects and a road map, and acknowledges the impact on seafarers
Training and manning
New fuels demand new competencies. The Strategy invites a seafarers' training and skills programme and asks the Organization to assess its instruments and training standards for a just transition
Developing States
The impact-assessment machinery, the capacity-building programmes and the trust funds exist because transport cost, connectivity and food security in LDCs and SIDS are directly exposed
Regional measures

Shipping was brought within the scope of the EU Emissions Trading System from 1 January 2024, so at this sitting a regional carbon cost already applies to some voyages while the global economic measure is still being developed - which is precisely the fragmentation a global measure is intended to prevent

blocks.p: The honest summary for a Chief Engineer is this. The short-term measures are law and are being enforced now. The mid-term measures are a defined programme of work with dates, not obligations - approval in 2025, adoption thereafter, entry into force around 2027. The long-term measures do not yet exist and will be shaped by the 2028 review. Anyone who describes the fuel standard or the pricing mechanism as a current requirement has confused a strategy with a regulation, and that is the single error this question is set to catch.

This is a 16-mark question with no printed limbs, which means the candidate supplies the structure and gets no help. The stem contains four separate asks - key objectives, key measures, the short-, mid- and long-term goals, and the impact on industry - and each is worth real marks. The commonest failure is to write four hundred words about net zero by 2050 and stop. The route here spends roughly a quarter of the answer on ambitions and checkpoints, a quarter on the measures by timeline, and a quarter on impact, which matches where the marks are.

Numbers are the cheapest marks on this question and they are all quotable: 40% intensity by 2030, 5% striving for 10% uptake by 2030, 20% striving for 30% absolute by 2030, 70% striving for 80% by 2040, net zero by or around 2050. Learn those five lines and half the question is already banked.

blocks.h: The distinction that carries the most marks

blocks.p: Levels of ambition are not the same as indicative checkpoints. The 40% figure is carbon intensity - emissions per transport work. The 20 / 30 and 70 / 80 figures are total annual emissions. An intensity target can be met while total emissions rise, if the fleet grows; an absolute checkpoint cannot. The 2023 Strategy is the first IMO instrument to set absolute figures at all, and a candidate who explains that difference has demonstrated understanding rather than recall.

ul: Treating the Strategy as a regulation. It is a resolution carrying a policy. Obligation comes only when a measure is adopted as a MARPOL Annex VI amendment and enters into force.
Saying 'carbon neutral by 2050'. The Strategy says net-zero GHG emissions by or around, i.e. close to, 2050. GHG, not CO2; and 'by or around', not a hard date.
Quoting the 2018 Initial Strategy's 50% by 2050 figure. That Strategy was revoked by MEPC.377(80) as from 7 July 2023.
Muddling intensity and absolute targets.
Describing the mid-term measures as though they were in force.
Inventing content for the long-term measures. The Strategy defines them as measures agreed beyond 2030, to be developed in the 2028 review, and says no more.
Forgetting the well-to-wake basis, which is what makes the fuel standard a life-cycle instrument rather than a funnel measurement.

The single biggest trap on this paper is answering this question with today's knowledge. At July 2024 the answer is MEPC.377(80) and nothing later. The IMO Net-Zero Framework, the Global Fuel Intensity mechanism and the approved basket all belong to 2025. Naming any of them dates the script instantly and, worse, misstates the law at the sitting.
MEPC 82 had not met. It sat 30 September to 4 October 2024, three months after this paper. Nothing may be attributed to it - including the 2024 SEEMP guidelines it adopted.

MEPC 81 had met, in March 2024, four months before. But the safe position is to describe the Strategy's own timetable rather than assert a session outcome: the basket was to be finalized at MEPC 81, approved at MEPC 83 in 2025 and adopted at an extraordinary session thereafter.
The review deadline is 1 January 2026, for the short-term measures under regulations 25.3 and 28.11. It is running at this sitting and has not reported.
FuelEU Maritime applies from 1 January 2025 and is future here. The EU ETS, by contrast, brought shipping into scope from 1 January 2024 and is operative - the two are constantly confused.
Which resolution, and when? MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80.
What happened to the 2018 Strategy? Revoked by the 2023 Strategy as from the date of adoption.
What are the two elements of the basket? A goal-based marine fuel standard on GHG intensity, and an economic element on the basis of a GHG emissions pricing mechanism.
What does well-to-wake mean and why does it matter? Life-cycle GHG intensity from production to use, so emissions are not shifted from the ship to the fuel's supply chain.
Is your ship complying with the Strategy today? No - the ship complies with EEXI, CII, SEEMP and the DCS under MARPOL Annex VI. Those are the short-term measures the Strategy refers to.
What is the difference between the 40% target and the 20% checkpoint? Intensity per transport work against total annual emissions.

blocks.p: Structure the whole answer as WHAT - HOW MUCH - BY WHEN - SO WHAT. WHAT: MEPC.377(80), 7 July 2023, revoking the 2018 Initial Strategy, a policy not a rule. HOW MUCH: four ambitions and two checkpoints - 40 intensity, 5 striving 10 uptake, 20 striving 30 absolute by 2030, 70 striving 80 by 2040, net zero by or around 2050. BY WHEN: short-term already in Annex VI, basket agreed by 2025 and in force around 2027, long-term after 2030 via the 2028 review. SO WHAT: fuels, newbuildings, existing tonnage, cost, contracts, safety, training, developing States, and the EU regional measure already running.
For the four ambitions, one line: new ships tighter, intensity down 40, clean energy 5 to 10, net zero around 2050. For the checkpoints: twenty-thirty by thirty, seventy-eighty by forty.

blocks.p: Everything asserted about the Strategy is read from the resolution itself, so within the Strategy there is no evidence gap. The uncertainty on this question is entirely temporal, and it runs one way: this is the question on which present-day knowledge is most likely to leak into a July 2024 answer. Three positions are therefore stated deliberately and are correct only for this sitting - that the basket had been neither approved nor adopted, that no mid-term measure was in force, and that the long-term measures did not yet exist. All three change during 2025 and none may be carried forward to a later sitting without re-derivation. Two smaller limits are also declared. No MEPC 81 or MEPC 82 outcome is asserted: the answer describes the Strategy's own timetable rather than what a session decided, because the Strategy is held and the session reports are not. And the EU ETS is named as regional context only, with no allowance price, surrender quantity or phase-in percentage, because no licensed text is held.

notes: THIS IS THE HIGHEST TEMPORAL RISK ON THE PAPER AND THE ANCHOR NAMES IT AS ONE OF TWO DECISIVE EXCLUSIONS. At July 2024 the answer to 'the IMO's revised strategy' is MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - almost exactly one year before the sitting - AND NOTHING LATER.

THE RISK IS NOT A DONOR, IT IS RECALL. This question has no donor, so there is no donor text to strip. The contamination route is present-day knowledge leaking in unmarked, which is harder to detect and is why the exclusions are enumerated rather than assumed.

PROHIBITED AND ABSENT - the IMO NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK and the GLOBAL FUEL INTENSITY (GFI) mechanism. Both belong to 2025, twelve to fifteen months after this sitting. Neither appears anywhere in this object.

PROHIBITED AND ABSENT - MEPC 83 (April 2025) and the APPROVAL of the basket of mid-term measures. The Strategy's own timetable places approval at MEPC 83 in spring 2025, which is nine months FUTURE at this sitting. The answer states the plan, not an outcome.
PROHIBITED AND ABSENT - MEPC 82 (30 September to 4 October 2024) and anything adopted there, including the 2024 SEEMP guidelines. MEPC 82 is three months FUTURE.

MEPC 81 (18-22 March 2024) IS PAST - four months before the sitting - AND IS HANDLED CONSERVATIVELY. The Strategy's follow-up table placed the interim impact-assessment report and the finalization of the basket at MEPC 81. The answer describes that PLAN and asserts no MEPC 81 outcome, because the Strategy is held in the corpus and the session report is not. The only MEPC 81 fact used anywhere on this paper is the identity and dates of resolution MEPC.385(81), read at source for Q3.
PROHIBITED AND ABSENT - FuelEU Maritime, which applies from 1 January 2025, six months future.
PROHIBITED AND ABSENT - the Hong Kong Convention, in force 26 June 2025, eleven months future. Recorded because ship recycling is an easy and wrong place to drift to on a decarbonisation question.

OPERATIVE AND CORRECTLY INCLUDED - the EU Emissions Trading System, into whose scope shipping was brought from 1 JANUARY 2024, six months before the sitting. It is named as regional context only, with no price, quantity or phase-in percentage asserted.
OPERATIVE AND CORRECTLY INCLUDED - EEXI, CII and SEEMP Part III, applying from 1 January 2023 under MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022.
THE 2018 INITIAL STRATEGY IS REVOKED, NOT SUPERSEDED-IN-PART. MEPC.377(80) paragraph 6 revokes MEPC.304(72) as from 7 July 2023. Its 50%-by-2050 figure must not appear, and it does not.

THE THREE SITTING-RELATIVE STATEMENTS. That the basket had been neither approved nor adopted; that no mid-term measure was in force; and that the long-term measures did not yet exist. All three are correct for July 2024, all three change during 2025, and all three are flagged for re-derivation rather than reuse.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One 16-mark question with four asks and no printed limbs. Identify the instrument and its key objectives; set out its measures; distinguish the short-, mid- and long-term goals; and evaluate the potential impact on the maritime industry. The fourth ask is an evaluation, not a recall, and carries real marks.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as a single block with no subpart split. The absence of limbs is itself the difficulty: the candidate must allocate, and the safe allocation is roughly a quarter each to ambitions and checkpoints, to the measures by timeline, to the impact, with the remainder on identification, principles and review.

quick_revision.recall_15s: MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, revoking the 2018 Initial Strategy. Vision - phase out as soon as possible, just and equitable transition. Four ambitions - strengthen new-ship efficiency; intensity down at least 40% by 2030 on 2008; zero or near-zero energy at least 5% striving 10% by 2030; net zero by or around 2050, well-to-wake. Two checkpoints - total emissions down at least 20% striving 30% by 2030 and 70% striving 80% by 2040. Short-term: EEDI, SEEMP, DCS, EEXI, CII, already in Annex VI, review by 1 January 2026. Mid-term basket by 2025: a goal-based marine fuel standard plus a GHG pricing mechanism - not approved, not adopted, not in force at this sitting. Long-term: beyond 2030 via the 2028 review.

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering with 2025 knowledge. At July 2024 the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the Global Fuel Intensity mechanism and the approved basket of mid-term measures do not exist - approval was scheduled for MEPC 83 in spring 2025 and adoption later still. questions.memory_cue: WHAT (1), HOW MUCH (3 and 4), BY WHEN (6, 7 and 8), SO WHAT (9). Objectives and principles fill 2 and 5.
questions.understand_first: Start from what kind of document this is, because everything else follows. It is not a rule. It is the Organization writing down where it intends shipping to be by 2030, 2040 and 2050, and what kind of measures it will build to get there. So the answer has three layers that must not be blurred: how much reduction is promised, what mechanisms are meant to deliver it, and when each mechanism arrives. The mechanisms that already exist work by measuring a ship's design efficiency and her operational carbon per unit of work, and they are law today. The mechanisms still being designed work differently - one would cap how much greenhouse gas each unit of energy she burns may carry, counted all the way back to how that fuel was made, and the other would put a price on what she emits. Those two are a plan with dates, not an obligation. And the reason the whole thing is slow is a genuine tension: every ship must be treated alike whatever her flag, yet the States least able to absorb higher freight costs are the ones the measures would hit hardest.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IMO revised GHG strategy question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Which instrument and what it replaced. 2 Vision and objectives. 3 Levels of ambition. 4 Indicative checkpoints. 5 Guiding principles. 6 Short-term measures. 7 The mid-term basket. 8 Long-term measures, timetable and review. 9 Impact on industry.
retrieval_cards.why: 16 marks with no printed limbs, so the candidate supplies the structure. Sections 3, 4, 6, 7 and 9 carry most of the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the four levels of ambition of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy.
retrieval_cards.answer: Carbon intensity of the ship to decline, through a review aimed at strengthening the energy efficiency design requirements for new ships. Carbon intensity of international shipping to decline - CO2 per transport work down by at least 40% by 2030 against 2008. Uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources to reach at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by 2030. GHG emissions to peak as soon as possible and reach net zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050.
retrieval_cards.why: Four ambitions, three numbers, all quotable - the highest mark density in the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between the levels of ambition and the indicative checkpoints?
retrieval_cards.answer: The levels of ambition are mainly INTENSITY targets - emissions per transport work - plus the uptake and net-zero commitments. The indicative checkpoints are ABSOLUTE: total annual GHG emissions from international shipping down at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, both against 2008. An intensity target can be met while total emissions rise if the fleet grows; an absolute checkpoint cannot.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the conceptual mark on the question and the distinction most candidates blur.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Strategy define short-, mid- and long-term measures?
retrieval_cards.answer: Short-term: measures finalized and agreed by the Committee between 2018 and 2023. Mid-term: the basket of measures to be finalized and agreed by 2025, with other candidate mid-term measures possible between 2023 and 2030. Long-term: measures finalized and agreed beyond 2030, to be developed as part of the 2028 review of the Strategy.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for short-, mid- and long-term goals; these are the Strategy's own definitions and they are dates, not topics.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two elements of the basket of candidate mid-term measures?
retrieval_cards.answer: A technical element - a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the phased reduction of the marine fuel's GHG intensity, measured well-to-wake. And an economic element, on the basis of a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. Candidate economic elements are assessed against specific criteria in the comprehensive impact assessment.
retrieval_cards.why: The two elements together are the core of the mid-term answer, and 'both, together' is the point.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At July 2024, what is the standing of the basket of mid-term measures?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither approved nor adopted, and nothing in force. The Strategy's own timetable set approval at MEPC 83 in spring 2025 and adoption at an extraordinary session about six months later, with entry into force sixteen months after adoption. The Net-Zero Framework and the Global Fuel Intensity mechanism belong to 2025 and must not appear in a July 2024 answer.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paper's single largest contamination risk and the position is correct only for this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which short-term measures is a ship actually complying with, and under what instrument?
retrieval_cards.answer: EEDI and SEEMP under MEPC.203(62); the IMO Data Collection System for fuel oil consumption under MEPC.278(70) for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above; and EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP including Part III under MEPC.328(76), the 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI. Their review must be completed by 1 January 2026.
retrieval_cards.why: It separates the Strategy, which binds nothing, from the Annex VI amendments, which bind the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which two guiding principles pull against each other, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: No more favourable treatment, from MARPOL, requires a measure to apply to every ship on the same terms whatever her flag. Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, from the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, recognises that States are not equally able to bear the cost. Reconciling the two is why the mid-term measures carry a comprehensive impact assessment and why they take so long to agree.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts a list of principles into an explanation of why the timetable is what it is.

blocks.h: (a) Ship identification number and the Continuous Synopsis Record
1. Where these requirements sit, and what they were written to solve

blocks.p: SOLAS chapter XI-1, Special measures to enhance maritime safety, is the chapter that attacks a particular problem: a ship whose identity can be changed. A substandard ship that is sold, renamed, re-flagged and re-classed can shed its record and start again clean, and both the port State and the next buyer lose the history that would have condemned her. Chapter XI-1 answers this by giving every ship a number that never changes and a document that travels with the hull rather than with the owner. At this sitting the operative text is the Consolidated Edition 2024, which carries all amendments in effect on 1 July 2024.

The chapter also carries regulation 1 (authorization of recognized organizations under the RO Code), regulation 2 (enhanced surveys, which is limb (b)), regulation 4 (port State control on operational requirements), regulation 6 (casualty investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code) and regulation 7 (portable atmosphere testing instruments).

blocks.h: 2. The ship identification number - regulation XI-1/3

ul: Application: all passenger ships of 100 gross tonnage and upwards and all cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage and upwards.

Every such ship is provided with an identification number conforming to the IMO ship identification number scheme adopted by the Organization. The number is allocated to the hull and does not change on sale, change of name or change of flag.
The number is inserted on the certificates, and on certified copies, issued under regulation I/12 or I/13.
It must be permanently marked in two places - one visible from outside, one accessible from inside.

rows: Externally visible (para 4.1)

On the stern; or either side of the hull amidships port and starboard above the deepest assigned load line; or either side of the superstructure port and starboard; or on the front of the superstructure; or, for passenger ships, on a horizontal surface visible from the air
Internally accessible (para 4.2)

On one of the end transverse bulkheads of the machinery spaces; or on one of the hatchways; or, for tankers, in the pump-room; or, for ships with ro-ro spaces, on one of the end transverse bulkheads of those spaces

ul: The marking must be plainly visible, clear of any other markings on the hull, and painted in a contrasting colour. The width of the characters is proportionate to the height.

It may be made by raised lettering, by cutting in, by centre-punching, or by any other equivalent method which ensures it is not easily expunged. That is the whole point of the internal marking: paint can be painted over, a punched or cut number cannot be removed without leaving evidence.
On ships built of material other than steel or metal, the Administration approves the method of marking.

Regulation XI-1/3-1 completes the identity set: every Company and registered owner also carries an identification number, under the IMO unique Company and registered owner identification number scheme, inserted on the Document of Compliance, the Safety Management Certificate and the ISPS certificates.

blocks.h: 3. The Continuous Synopsis Record - regulation XI-1/5

blocks.p: Every ship to which chapter I applies is issued with a Continuous Synopsis Record, issued by the Administration - not by class, not by the Company - to each ship entitled to fly its flag. Its purpose is stated in the regulation itself: to provide an on-board record of the history of the ship in respect of the information recorded in it. For ships built before 1 July 2004 the history runs from 1 July 2004.
It must contain at least the following:

ol: the flag State the ship is entitled to fly;
the date of registration with that State;
the ship's identification number under regulation 3;
the name of the ship;
the port of registry;
the name and registered address of the registered owner(s);
the registered owner identification number;
the name and registered address of any registered bareboat charterer(s);
the name of the Company as defined in regulation IX/1, its registered address, and the addresses from which it carries out its safety management activities;
the Company identification number;
the name of every classification society with which the ship is classed;
who issued the Document of Compliance, and who audited for it;
who issued the Safety Management Certificate, and who audited for it;
who issued the International Ship Security Certificate, and who verified for it;
the date on which the ship ceased to be registered with that State.

blocks.h: 4. Keeping the CSR - the rules that give it its value

ul: Changes to entries 3.4 to 3.12 are recorded so as to give the current position together with the history of the changes. The Administration issues a revised CSR or amendments not later than three months from the date of change, and, pending that, requires the Company or the master to amend the CSR, the Company then informing the Administration without delay.
The CSR is in English, French or Spanish, with a translation into the Administration's own language if desired, and in the format developed by the Organization.
Previous entries may never be modified, deleted, erased or defaced. This is the provision that makes it a record rather than a status sheet.
On transfer of flag, sale, change of bareboat charterer or change of Company, the CSR is left on board.

Before a transfer of flag the Company notifies its Administration of the incoming flag, the outgoing Contracting Government transmits to the new Administration a copy covering its own period together with any earlier CSRs, and the new Administration appends the previous records to the one it issues.
The CSR is kept on board and available for inspection at all times.

blocks.h: 5. Why the two together enhance maritime safety

ul: They defeat identity laundering. A permanent number plus an unbroken, appended history means a ship cannot escape her record by changing name, owner, flag or class.

They give the port State control officer an immediate picture before he inspects: how often the ship has changed flag or class, whether she has passed through several owners quickly, and who audited her management system. Those are classic targeting indicators, and they are on the bridge in one document.
They make flag-hopping and class-hopping visible rather than invisible, which deters both.
They tie the ship to a Company and to a registered owner by number, so responsibility under the ISM Code can be traced to a real entity even through a chain of single-ship companies.
They support casualty investigation and detention follow-up, since the history is on board and does not depend on the cooperation of a former owner.
Because the number is on the certificates as well as on the hull, they make certificate fraud harder: the paper and the steel have to agree.

blocks.h: 6. What the ESP is, and which ships are subject to it

blocks.p: The Enhanced Survey Programme is a mandatory, prescribed programme of hull inspections that goes far beyond a general survey: it fixes, ship type by ship type and age band by age band, exactly which spaces must be entered, how much of the structure must be examined within arm's reach, how many thickness readings must be taken and where, and which tanks must be pressure tested. It exists because bulk carriers and oil tankers had the worst structural loss record of any ship types, and because those losses were caused by wastage and cracking that a walk-round survey does not find.

ul: SOLAS regulation XI-1/2 requires bulk carriers as defined in regulation IX/1.6 and oil tankers as defined in regulation II-1/2.22 to be subject to an enhanced programme of inspections in accordance with the 2011 ESP Code, adopted by the Assembly as resolution A.1049(27) on 30 November 2011, as may be amended.
That is how the Code becomes mandatory: not because it is called a Code, but because regulation XI-1/2 says so - and its amendments must be adopted and brought into force under SOLAS article VIII.
The Code is organised as Annex A for bulk carriers - Part A for single-side skin construction, Part B for double-side skin - and Annex B for oil tankers, with a part for double-hull tankers.

Annex A Part A applies to self-propelled bulk carriers of 500 gross tonnage and above other than double-side skin bulk carriers. For hybrid arrangements, the double-side skin part governs the double-side skin holds and their wing spaces.

The surveys are carried out during the surveys prescribed by SOLAS regulation I/10 - they are not an extra survey regime bolted on, but a defined depth for the annual, intermediate and renewal surveys.
Regulation XI-1/2-1 allows cargo ships not subject to the ESP Code to harmonize their intermediate and renewal survey periods with the ESP Code periods.

blocks.h: 7. The key components of an enhanced survey

rows: Survey programme and planning meeting

A written survey programme prepared by the owner in cooperation with the society before the renewal survey begins, using the survey planning questionnaire, and a planning meeting held between the surveyor, the owner's representative and the thickness measurement operator before the survey starts
Documentation on board

The survey report file - survey reports, condition evaluation reports and thickness measurement records - plus supporting documents: main structural plans, previous repair history, cargo and ballast history, the owner's inspection reports, and coating and corrosion-prevention records. The surveyor reviews these before the survey
Conditions for survey and access

Spaces cleaned, gas-freed, ventilated and lit; safe access provided - staging, rafts or boats within the limits allowed, or approved alternative means. Nothing is examined that cannot be safely reached
Overall survey
A survey of a space to report on the overall condition of the hull structure and to determine the extent of additional close-up survey required
Close-up survey
Structural detail examined within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor - normally within reach of hand. This is the heart of the programme; the required extent is tabulated by age band
Thickness measurements

Taken by a company certified for the purpose, to prescribed procedures and reporting, at prescribed locations including transverse sections. Extended measurement is required in areas of substantial corrosion
Tank pressure testing
Prescribed extent of testing of ballast and cargo tank boundaries
Dry-dock survey
Examination of the bottom and other parts normally inaccessible afloat, in conjunction with the renewal survey
Reporting and evaluation
Evaluation of the survey report and issue of a Condition Evaluation Report, which goes into the survey report file and travels with the ship

blocks.p: Four definitions carry most of the technical weight and are worth knowing exactly. A transverse section is the cross section of the hull perpendicular to the centreline, including all longitudinal members. Suspect areas are locations showing substantial corrosion or considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage. Substantial corrosion is wastage in excess of 75% of the allowable margins but still within acceptable limits - and for ships built to the IACS Common Structural Rules it is a measured thickness between tnet + 0.5 mm and tnet. Coating condition is graded GOOD (only minor spot rusting), FAIR (local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections, or light rusting, over 20% or more of the area under consideration), or POOR (general breakdown of coating over 20% or more of the area, or hard scale at 10% or more). The coating grade is not cosmetic: a ballast tank whose coating falls to POOR moves into annual internal examination, so coating condition drives survey frequency.

ul: To detect structural deterioration - wastage, cracking, coating breakdown and buckling - before it becomes a casualty, in the two ship types whose structural failures have historically been sudden and catastrophic.
To define a minimum extent of examination that is the same for every ship of a given type and age, so that a survey means the same thing whoever performs it and wherever it is performed.
To make condition measurable rather than impressionistic, through thickness measurement by a certified company and through graded coating condition.

To escalate automatically: where substantial corrosion or structural defect is found, the survey is extended and further close-up survey and measurement are required. The programme adapts to what the ship is actually telling the surveyor.
To force planning and owner participation rather than turn-up-and-look, through the survey programme, the planning meeting and the owner's own inspection reports.

To build a continuous structural history in the survey report file and the Condition Evaluation Report, so successive surveys measure a trend rather than a snapshot - which, like the CSR in limb (a), is the theme of this whole chapter: the ship's record must survive the change of owner.

blocks.p: Both limbs ask three things and are marked as one. Limb (a) is really 'ship ID number' + 'CSR' + 'why they enhance safety', and the third of those is where most candidates run out of paper. Do not leave section 5 to a single sentence: the significance question is worth as much as the description and it is the part that cannot be looked up on board. Limb (b) is 'what it is' + 'which ships' + 'key components' + 'objectives' - four asks in eight marks - which is why the components belong in a table and the objectives in a list.

The single most reliable way to lose marks on this question is to describe the CSR without the rules that give it its value: never erased, left on board on sale, previous records appended by the new flag. A CSR that could be replaced on change of flag would be worthless, and the examiner is testing whether you know why.

Chapter XI-1 is about continuity of identity and continuity of record. Limb (a) makes the ship's identity and her documentary history survive a change of owner. Limb (b) makes her structural history survive it too - the survey report file, the thickness measurement records and the Condition Evaluation Report follow the hull, not the company. Say that once and both limbs become one argument instead of two lists.

ul: Giving one marking location. There are two - externally visible and internally accessible - and the two heights differ: 200 mm and 100 mm.
Saying the CSR is issued by class or by the Company. It is issued by the Administration.
Saying the CSR is surrendered or replaced on change of flag. It is left on board, and the new Administration appends the previous records.
Writing that the ESP applies to 'all ships'. It applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers, by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2.
Treating the ESP as a separate survey. It is the prescribed depth of the surveys already required by regulation I/10.
Describing close-up survey as 'a detailed look'. It has a definition - within reach of hand - and quoting it costs one line and earns a mark.
Guessing a percentage for substantial corrosion. It is wastage in excess of 75% of the allowable margins, still within acceptable limits.

The SOLAS edition. At this sitting the operative text is the Consolidated Edition 2024: the November 2022 amendments, resolution MSC.521(106), entered into force 1 July 2024. Those amendments introduced chapter XV for ships carrying industrial personnel; they do not amend chapter XI-1, so the substance of this answer is unchanged - but a candidate who says chapter XI-1 was amended on 1 July 2024 is wrong.

Which regulation is which. XI-1/1 RO Code, XI-1/2 enhanced surveys, XI-1/3 ship identification number, XI-1/3-1 Company and registered owner number, XI-1/4 PSC on operational requirements, XI-1/5 CSR, XI-1/6 casualty investigation, XI-1/7 atmosphere testing instrument. Getting 3 and 5 the right way round is worth doing.
The oral favourite: 'who issues the CSR and who keeps it?' The Administration issues it; the ship keeps it on board, available for inspection at all times.
Coating condition is not cosmetic. Expect to be asked what happens when a ballast tank coating is found POOR - it brings the space into annual internal examination.
The IMO number belongs to the hull. It does not change on sale, rename or re-flag; the Company and registered owner numbers do change when those parties change.
Where is your ship's IMO number marked internally, and what height? On an end transverse bulkhead of the machinery space (or a hatchway, or the pump-room on a tanker), minimum 100 mm.

What must you do if the Company changes tomorrow? The entry is amended, the Administration issues a revised CSR within three months, and pending that the master or Company amends it and informs the Administration without delay.
Which ships are subject to the ESP Code, and under what regulation? Bulk carriers (IX/1.6) and oil tankers (II-1/2.22), under SOLAS XI-1/2.
What is a close-up survey? Structural detail within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor - normally within reach of hand.
Who may take the thickness measurements? A thickness measurement company certified for the purpose, working to the Code's procedures and reporting requirements.
What is a Condition Evaluation Report? The output of the evaluation of a renewal survey, kept in the survey report file, which stays with the ship.

blocks.p: Limb (a) in three words: NUMBER - RECORD - WHY. The number: who (100 GT passenger / 300 GT cargo), where (outside 200, inside 100), how (contrasting, not easily expunged). The record: who issues (Administration), what is in it (flag, registry, owner, charterer, Company, class, DOC, SMC, ISSC), how it is kept (never erased, left on board, appended). Then why: identity laundering, PSC targeting, ISM traceability.

Limb (b) in four: WHO - PLAN - LOOK - MEASURE. Who: bulk carriers and tankers under XI-1/2 and A.1049(27). Plan: survey programme, planning meeting, survey report file, conditions and access. Look: overall survey, then close-up within reach of hand. Measure: thickness by a certified company, tank testing, substantial corrosion at 75% of allowable margins, coating GOOD / FAIR / POOR - and then the Condition Evaluation Report that carries it all forward.

blocks.p: Both limbs are written from primary text read at source this session, so the evidence position is strong. Three limits are stated rather than concealed. First, the IMO ship identification number scheme and the unique Company and registered owner identification number scheme are identified in the regulation's own footnotes but are not held in the MIW corpus, so nothing about the composition of the numbers is asserted beyond what the regulation itself says. Second, no IACS unified requirement or class rule is cited anywhere - MIW holds no IACS text - which is why the answer describes coating-driven escalation in the Code's own terms rather than quoting a class rule. Third, the ESP Code has been amended since 2011 and SOLAS regulation XI-1/2 admits amendments adopted under article VIII; the structure, definitions and components stated here are taken from the base Code as read, and a later sitting must re-check whether an amendment has altered any tabulated extent.

notes: THIS IS THE QUESTION THE PAPER'S TEMPORAL BOUNDARY IS LIVE ON, AND IT IS RESOLVED AT SOURCE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024 foreword records that the November 2022 amendments, resolution MSC.521(106), ENTERED INTO FORCE 1 JULY 2024, and the edition carries all amendments in effect on that date. 1 July precedes every possible July sitting date, so the 2024 edition is operative for the whole month and NO DAY-LEVEL ASSUMPTION IS MADE OR NEEDED.

THE SECOND HALF OF THE CHECK - WHAT MSC.521(106) ACTUALLY DID. The anchor left this expressly to this record. MSC.521(106) is the amendment set that introduced SOLAS CHAPTER XV, safety measures for ships carrying industrial personnel, alongside the IP Code (MSC.527(106)); the 2024 edition's own unified interpretation for chapter XV attributes regulations XV/3.2, 3.3 and 5.1 to MSC.521(106). It does NOT amend chapter XI-1. The consequence is precise: the EDITION changed on 1 July 2024, the SUBSTANCE of chapter XI-1 did not, and this answer cites the 2024 edition without claiming any change to the regulations it relies on.

CONTRAST WITH THE JUNE 2024 SITTING. QP2406 sat before the boundary and correctly recorded the 2024 consolidated edition as future. Both statements are right and they are not in conflict; the boundary runs between the two papers.

THE ESP CODE EDITION. A.1049(27) was adopted 30 November 2011 and became effective on entry into force of the associated chapter XI-1 amendments. It is the instrument named by regulation XI-1/2 at this sitting. Amendments to it must be adopted and brought into force under SOLAS article VIII; the structure, application and definitions relied on here are read from the base Code and no amended tabulated extent is asserted.
MEPC 81 (March 2024) AND MSC 108 (May 2024) BOTH PRECEDE THE SITTING AND ARE CHECKED. Neither bears on chapter XI-1, on the ship identification number, on the CSR or on the ESP Code.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs, each with an internal three-part structure. (a) State the requirements for the ship identification number and for the CSR under chapter XI-1, then EXPLAIN their significance for safety - the third part is a reasoning task, not a recall task. (b) Define the ESP, identify the ships subject to it, then set out its key components and its objectives.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8, printed against each limb. Within limb (a) the significance question carries real weight and is the part most often truncated; within limb (b) four separate asks share eight marks, which forces a compact tabular treatment of the components.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: Regulation-accurate detail - the two marking locations and their two minimum heights, the CSR's issuer and its content, the ships subject to the ESP and the instrument that makes it mandatory - followed by an understanding of WHY: that chapter XI-1 exists to stop a ship shedding her identity and her record.

technical_ambiguities: The stem writes 'Enhanced Survey Program' where the instrument is the 'Enhanced Programme of Inspections during Surveys'. The answer uses the Code's own title once and the examiner's term thereafter, rather than correcting the stem

'Key components' is not a defined term; it is read as the elements of the programme the Code itself sections - planning, documentation, access, overall and close-up survey, thickness measurement, tank testing, reporting

quick_revision.recall_15s: Chapter XI-1 keeps identity and record continuous. Reg 3: IMO number, passenger 100 GT / cargo 300 GT, marked outside 200 mm and inside 100 mm, contrasting, not easily expunged. Reg 5: CSR issued by the Administration, fifteen items, revised within three months, never erased, left on board on sale, previous records appended, always available for inspection. Reg 2: bulk carriers and oil tankers, 2011 ESP Code A.1049(27) - survey programme, planning meeting, overall then close-up within reach of hand, thickness measurement by a certified company, substantial corrosion at 75% of allowable margins, coating GOOD / FAIR / POOR, Condition Evaluation Report.
critical_numbers: Ship identification number: passenger ships 100 GT and upwards, cargo ships 300 GT and upwards
Marking heights: 200 mm externally visible, 100 mm internally accessible
CSR: revised or amended not later than 3 months from the date of change
CSR history for pre-2004 ships runs from 1 July 2004
ESP Code Annex A Part A: self-propelled bulk carriers of 500 gross tonnage and above

Coating POOR: general breakdown over 20% or more of the area, or hard scale at 10% or more
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS regulations XI-1/3 (ship identification number) and XI-1/5 (Continuous Synopsis Record); SOLAS regulation XI-1/2, which makes the 2011 ESP Code (resolution A.1049(27)) mandatory for bulk carriers and oil tankers.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the CSR is surrendered or replaced when the ship changes flag. It is LEFT ON BOARD, and the new Administration appends the previous records to the one it issues. The second trap at this sitting is the SOLAS edition: MSC.521(106) entered into force 1 July 2024 and made the Consolidated Edition 2024 operative, but it introduced chapter XV and did not amend chapter XI-1.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is NUMBER (2), RECORD (3), KEEPING (4), WHY (5). Limb (b) is WHO (6), COMPONENTS (7), OBJECTIVES (8).
questions.understand_first: Think about what happens to a bad ship when she is sold. New name, new owner, new flag, new class - and, without this chapter, no way for anyone to know what she was before. So the Convention does two things. It gives the hull a number that never changes and marks it where paint cannot hide it, and it gives the ship a running history book that stays on board when the owner leaves, with earlier pages never removed and earlier books attached to the new one. The second limb is the same idea applied to steel rather than paperwork: for the two ship types that used to break up and sink, the survey is not left to a walk-round but is prescribed in advance - which spaces, how close, how many thickness readings - and the results are written into a file that follows the hull. Identity, paperwork and structure are all made to outlive the owner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the ship identification number, CSR and ESP question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What chapter XI-1 is for. 2 The ship identification number. 3 The CSR and its content. 4 How the CSR is kept and transferred. 5 Why both enhance safety. 6 What the ESP is and which ships. 7 Key components. 8 Objectives.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. Sections 1-5 are limb (a), 6-8 are limb (b), and section 5 is the part candidates truncate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where and at what size must the ship identification number be permanently marked?
retrieval_cards.answer: Two places. Externally visible - stern, or either side of the hull amidships above the deepest assigned load line, or either side or the front of the superstructure, or for passenger ships a horizontal surface visible from the air - minimum 200 mm. Internally accessible - an end transverse bulkhead of the machinery space, a hatchway, the pump-room on a tanker, or an end transverse bulkhead of the ro-ro spaces - minimum 100 mm. Plainly visible, clear of other markings, contrasting colour, and made so it is not easily expunged.
retrieval_cards.why: The two locations and the two heights are the most examinable facts in limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who issues the Continuous Synopsis Record, and what happens to it when the ship is sold or changes flag?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Administration issues it to each ship entitled to fly its flag. On sale, transfer of flag, change of bareboat charterer or change of Company it is LEFT ON BOARD. The Company notifies its Administration of the incoming flag; the outgoing Contracting Government transmits a copy covering its period together with any earlier records; and the new Administration appends the previous records to the CSR it issues. Previous entries are never modified, deleted, erased or defaced.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the mechanism that makes the CSR worth having, and the standard place candidates get it wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships are subject to the Enhanced Survey Programme, and what makes it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Bulk carriers as defined in SOLAS regulation IX/1.6 and oil tankers as defined in regulation II-1/2.22. SOLAS regulation XI-1/2 requires them to be surveyed in accordance with the 2011 ESP Code, adopted by the Assembly as resolution A.1049(27) on 30 November 2011, as may be amended. The Code is mandatory because that regulation says so, not because it is called a Code.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks 'what type of vessels' and the marks are in the SOLAS definitions and the enabling regulation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define overall survey, close-up survey and substantial corrosion.
retrieval_cards.answer: Overall survey: a survey intended to report on the overall condition of the hull structure and to determine the extent of additional close-up survey. Close-up survey: a survey where the details of structural components are within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor, normally within reach of hand. Substantial corrosion: wastage in excess of 75% of the allowable margins but within acceptable limits - for ships built to the IACS Common Structural Rules, a measured thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net.
retrieval_cards.why: These three definitions carry most of the technical marks in limb (b) and each is one line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is coating condition graded under the ESP Code, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: GOOD - only minor spot rusting. FAIR - local breakdown of coating at edges of stiffeners and weld connections, or light rusting, over 20% or more of the area under consideration, but less than POOR. POOR - general breakdown of coating over 20% or more of the area, or hard scale at 10% or more. It matters because coating condition drives survey frequency and the extent of close-up survey and thickness measurement.
retrieval_cards.why: The grades are examinable verbatim and the consequence is the oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the key components of an enhanced survey.
retrieval_cards.answer: Survey programme and survey planning meeting; documentation on board - survey report file and supporting documents; conditions for survey and safe access; overall survey; close-up survey; thickness measurement by a certified company; tank pressure testing; dry-dock survey; and reporting and evaluation, including the Condition Evaluation Report.
retrieval_cards.why: Nine components, one table, eight marks shared with three other asks - this is a list, not an essay.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At July 2024, what is the operative SOLAS edition, and did the amendment that made it operative change chapter XI-1?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Consolidated Edition 2024, which carries all amendments in effect on 1 July 2024. The November 2022 amendments, resolution MSC.521(106), entered into force on that date - but they introduced chapter XV on ships carrying industrial personnel, together with the IP Code. They do not amend chapter XI-1, whose substance is unchanged across the boundary.
retrieval_cards.why: The edition boundary falls on this sitting. Getting the edition right without inventing a chapter XI-1 amendment is the precise position.

questions.verification_status: This question rests on primary text read at source and it carries one of the paper's two decisive temporal exclusions. THE OPERATIVE EDITION WAS ESTABLISHED AT SOURCE, NOT ASSUMED: the corpus holds TWO consolidated texts of the Convention in the same folder. The one used here states on its own title page that it is the 'Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, as amended - Consolidated text established by the International Labour Office, including the Amendments of 2014, 2016 and 2018 to the Code of the Convention', printed 2020. The other also carries the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session (2022). THE 2022 SET DOES NOT ENTER INTO FORCE UNTIL 23 DECEMBER 2024, FIVE MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING, so the 2018 consolidation is the operative edition and the 2022 text was read only to know what to exclude. That is exactly the trap the paper anchor records at section 4.1: the later file is present, readable and inapplicable. Title 5 was read in full from the operative text - the introductory paragraphs, Regulations 5.1.1 to 5.1.6 with Standards A5.1.1 to A5.1.5, Regulations 5.2.1 and 5.2.2 with Standards A5.2.1 and A5.2.2, Regulation 5.3 and Standard A5.3, and Appendix A5-I. Every interval, every threshold and every trigger stated in this answer is taken from that reading. No regional memorandum of understanding is named and no detention statistic is asserted, because MIW holds no such documentation.
sources: P1 PRIMARY - Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, as amended, consolidated text established by the International Labour Office including the Amendments of 2014, 2016 and 2018, read at source. Title 5, Compliance and enforcement, read in full: the introductory paragraphs, including the rule that Article VI paragraphs 3 and 4 - substantial equivalence - do not apply to Part A of the Code in this Title.

P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.1 and Standard A5.1.1: each Member responsible for implementation on ships that fly its flag; an effective system of inspection and certification; authorization of recognized organizations while remaining fully responsible; the certificate and declaration as prima facie evidence; reporting under article 22 of the ILO Constitution; and the requirement that every ship carry a copy of the Convention.

P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.2 and Standard A5.1.2: recognition of organizations for competency and independence; the four capability tests; the minimum content of an inspection authorization; the oversight system; and the current list of recognized organizations provided to the International Labour Office and made publicly available.

P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.3 and Standard A5.1.3: application to ships of 500 gross tonnage or over on international voyages or operating from or between ports in another country, and to any other ship at the shipowner's request; certificate validity not exceeding five years; intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; the renewal and extension rules; the interim certificate for a period not exceeding six months and the four verifications required for it; the two-part structure of the DMLC; carriage, posting and English translation; the five grounds on which a certificate ceases to be valid; and withdrawal. Appendix A5-I, the sixteen matters that must be inspected and approved before certification, read at source.

P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.4 and Standard A5.1.4: the effective and coordinated system of regular inspections; sufficient qualified inspectors; the inspection interval which shall in no case exceed three years; investigation of a complaint that is not manifestly unfounded; the inspectors' independence, powers of board, examination and prohibition from sailing; right of appeal; confidentiality of the source of a complaint; conflict-of-interest prohibitions; reporting to the competent authority with a copy to the master and a copy posted on board; the annual report published within six months of the year end; a major-incident report within one month of the conclusion of the investigation; avoidance of unreasonable detention; compensation with the burden of proof on the complainant; and adequate penalties.

P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.5 and Standard A5.1.5: on-board complaint procedures; the prohibition and penalisation of victimization; resolution at the lowest level with the right to complain directly to the master and to external authorities; the right to be accompanied or represented; and the copy of the procedures given to every seafarer with the flag State and country-of-residence contacts and the name of a person on board who can give confidential impartial advice.
P1 PRIMARY - Regulation 5.1.6: an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty leading to injury or loss of life, the report normally made public.
