blocks.h: 1. Where these obligations live, and the one rule that makes Title 5 different

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is built in three layers: Articles, Regulations, and a Code in two parts - Part A, mandatory Standards, and Part B, non-mandatory Guidelines. Compliance and enforcement is Title 5, and it divides exactly as this question does: Regulation 5.1 flag State responsibilities, Regulation 5.2 port State responsibilities, and Regulation 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities.

One rule in the introduction to Title 5 is worth stating first because it is the mark most candidates miss. Elsewhere in the Convention, Article VI paragraphs 3 and 4 allow a Member to implement Part A of the Code through substantially equivalent provisions. That permission does not apply to Part A of the Code in Title 5. Enforcement machinery must be implemented as written - a State may run its labour standards its own way, but it may not run its enforcement its own way. Title 5 also states that seafarers and shipowners are equal before the law and entitled to its equal protection, and that Title 5 does not itself determine legal jurisdiction or venue.

blocks.h: 2. Flag State - the general responsibility and the system it must build

ul: Each Member is responsible for ensuring implementation of its obligations on ships that fly its flag (Regulation 5.1.1).

It must establish an effective system for the inspection and certification of maritime labour conditions, so that working and living conditions meet, and continue to meet, the standards of the Convention.
It must set clear objectives and standards for the administration of that system and adequate procedures for assessing whether they are being attained (Standard A5.1.1).
It must require every ship flying its flag to carry a copy of the Convention on board.
It reports on the system, including the method used to assess its effectiveness, to the International Labour Office under article 22 of the ILO Constitution.

blocks.h: 3. Recognized organizations - what may be delegated, and what may not

ul: The Member may authorize public institutions or other organizations - in practice classification societies - to carry out inspections, to issue certificates, or both. In all cases the Member remains fully responsible for the inspection and certification of the seafarers' conditions. Delegation of work is permitted; delegation of responsibility is not.

An organization is recognized only after the competent authority has reviewed its competency and independence and satisfied itself that it has the necessary expertise in the relevant aspects of the Convention and knowledge of ship operations; the ability to maintain and update that expertise; knowledge of the Convention, national law and relevant international instruments; and appropriate size, structure, experience and capability for the authorization given.
Any inspection authorization must, as a minimum, empower the organization to require the rectification of deficiencies it identifies and to carry out inspections at the request of a port State.

The Member must establish a system to ensure the adequacy of the organization's work and procedures for communication with and oversight of it, and must give the International Labour Office a current list of its recognized organizations and the functions each is authorized to perform, which the Office makes publicly available.

blocks.h: 4. The Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC

blocks.p: Certification is compulsory for ships of 500 gross tonnage or over engaged on international voyages, and for ships of 500 gross tonnage or over flying a Member's flag and operating from a port, or between ports, in another country. Any other ship may be certified at the shipowner's request. Together the two documents are prima facie evidence that the ship has been duly inspected and meets the requirements to the extent certified.

rows: Validity
Not exceeding five years, issued by the competent authority or an authorized recognized organization, with a publicly available record of the certificate
Intermediate inspection

Between the second and third anniversary dates where one is carried out on a five-year certificate; equal in scope and depth to a renewal inspection; the certificate is endorsed on satisfactory completion
Renewal

Completed within three months before expiry - new certificate runs five years from the old expiry date; completed earlier than that - five years from completion. Extension of up to five months where the ship is found compliant but the certificate cannot yet be issued
Interim certificate

Not exceeding six months, for a new ship on delivery, a change of flag, or a shipowner assuming responsibility for a ship new to it. Requires inspection so far as reasonable and practicable, adequate shipowner procedures, a master familiar with the Convention, and the information for a DMLC. No second interim certificate, and no DMLC is required during its currency
DMLC Part I

Drawn up by the competent authority: the list of matters to be inspected, the national requirements implementing the Convention, ship-type specific requirements, any substantial equivalences, and any Title 3 exemption
DMLC Part II

Drawn up by the shipowner: the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections and the measures proposed for continuous improvement. Certified by the competent authority or the recognized organization
Carriage

Both documents carried on board with an English translation where not in English, a copy posted in a conspicuous place available to seafarers, and copies available on request to seafarers, flag State inspectors, port State authorized officers and shipowners' and seafarers' representatives

blocks.p: The certificate ceases to be valid if the required inspections are not completed or the certificate is not endorsed, on a change of flag, when the shipowner ceases to be responsible for the ship's operation, or when substantial changes are made to structure or equipment covered in Title 3. It is withdrawn where there is evidence of non-compliance and required corrective action has not been taken, the authority having regard to the seriousness or the frequency of the deficiencies. The sixteen matters that must be inspected and approved before certification are listed in Appendix A5-I and run from minimum age and medical certification through hours of work or rest, manning, accommodation, food and catering, health and safety, on-board complaint procedures and payment of wages to the two financial security requirements.

ul: The Member verifies through an effective and coordinated system of regular inspections, monitoring and other control measures that ships flying its flag comply.

It appoints a sufficient number of qualified inspectors, with the training, competence, terms of reference, powers, status and independence to do the work - independent of changes of government and of improper external influences.
Inspections take place at the intervals required for certification, and the interval shall in no case exceed three years.
On a complaint that is not manifestly unfounded, or evidence of non-conformity or of serious deficiencies in the measures set out in the DMLC, the Member investigates and ensures remedial action.

Inspectors may board a ship flying the Member's flag, carry out any examination, test or inquiry they consider necessary, require rectification, and - where deficiencies constitute a serious breach or a significant danger to seafarers' safety, health or security - prohibit the ship from leaving port. Any such action carries a right of appeal to a judicial or administrative authority.

Inspectors have discretion to advise instead of prosecuting where there is no clear breach endangering seafarers and no history of similar breaches; must treat the source of a complaint as confidential and give no intimation that an inspection followed from one; and must have no direct or indirect interest in anything they inspect and reveal no commercial secrets.

Every inspection is reported to the competent authority, with a copy in English or the ship's working language to the master and a copy posted on the notice board for the seafarers. Records are kept, an annual report is published within six months of the year end, and a report following a major incident goes to the authority within one month of the conclusion of the investigation.

All reasonable efforts are made to avoid a ship being unreasonably detained or delayed; compensation is payable for wrongful exercise of the inspectors' powers, the burden of proof being on the complainant; and adequate penalties must exist and be enforced for breaches and for obstructing inspectors.

blocks.h: 6. On-board complaint procedures and marine casualties

ul: Every ship must have on-board procedures for the fair, effective and expeditious handling of seafarer complaints (Regulation 5.1.5), and the Member must prohibit and penalize any kind of victimization of a seafarer for filing one.

The procedures seek resolution at the lowest level possible, but in all cases the seafarer has the right to complain directly to the master and, where he considers it necessary, to appropriate external authorities.

The seafarer has the right to be accompanied or represented, and every seafarer receives, with the employment agreement, a copy of the procedures - including the contact details of the competent authority in the flag State and in the seafarer's country of residence, and the name of a person on board who can give confidential, impartial advice.

Under Regulation 5.1.6 the flag State must hold an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty leading to injury or loss of life involving a ship flying its flag, and the final report is normally made public.

Every foreign ship calling in the normal course of its business or for operational reasons in the port of a Member may be inspected, under Article V paragraph 4, to review compliance with the Convention including seafarers' rights (Regulation 5.2.1).

But the Member shall accept the Maritime Labour Certificate and the DMLC as prima facie evidence of compliance, and accordingly the inspection shall be limited to a review of the certificate and the declaration except in the circumstances specified in the Code. That is the default, and it is a real constraint on the officer.
Inspections are carried out by authorized officers, in accordance with the Code and other applicable international arrangements governing port State control.
Any inspection is limited to verifying conformity with the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code. Part B is guidance and cannot found a deficiency.
The Member must operate an effective port State inspection and monitoring system and report on it to the International Labour Office.

blocks.h: 8. The more detailed inspection, and detention

blocks.p: A more detailed inspection may be carried out where the authorized officer finds that:

ol: the required documents are not produced or maintained, are falsely maintained, do not contain the required information, or are otherwise invalid;
there are clear grounds for believing that the working and living conditions do not conform to the Convention;
there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship has changed flag to avoid compliance; or
there is a complaint alleging that specific conditions do not conform.

blocks.p: Such an inspection shall in any case be carried out where the conditions believed or alleged to be defective could constitute a clear hazard to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or where the officer has grounds to believe the deficiencies are a serious breach. Under grounds 1 to 3 the detailed inspection covers in principle the matters in Appendix A5-III; on a complaint it is generally limited to the scope of the complaint, though the complaint may itself provide clear grounds for a wider inspection.

Deficiencies are brought forthwith to the master with deadlines for rectification. Where they are significant, or relate to a complaint, the officer also brings them to the appropriate seafarers' and shipowners' organizations in the port State, and may notify a representative of the flag State and provide the next port of call with the information. A copy of the report, with any flag State reply, may be transmitted to the Director-General of the International Labour Office.

Detention has two grounds and only two. Where a more detailed inspection shows non-conformity and either (a) the conditions on board are clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or (b) the non-conformity constitutes a serious or repeated breach of the Convention including seafarers' rights, the officer shall take steps to ensure the ship does not proceed to sea until the non-conformities are rectified or until he has accepted a plan of action to rectify them and is satisfied it will be implemented expeditiously. If the ship is prevented from sailing he must forthwith notify the flag State, invite its representative to be present if possible, request a reply within a prescribed deadline, and inform the shipowners' and seafarers' organizations in the port State. Every possible effort must be made to avoid undue detention or delay, and compensation is payable for loss or damage from undue detention, the burden of proof lying on the complainant.

blocks.h: 9. Onshore complaint handling, and the third leg of Title 5

ul: Under Regulation 5.2.2 a seafarer on a ship calling at a port may report an alleged breach to an authorized officer in that port, who undertakes an initial investigation.
The officer considers, where appropriate, whether the on-board complaint procedures have been explored, may conduct a more detailed inspection, and seeks to promote resolution at ship-board level.

If the investigation reveals a non-conformity within the detention grounds, those grounds apply. Otherwise, if the complaint is not resolved on board, the officer forthwith notifies the flag State, seeking advice and a corrective plan of action within a prescribed deadline.

If it is still unresolved, the port State transmits the report to the Director-General of the International Labour Office, with the flag State's reply, and informs the shipowners' and seafarers' organizations. Statistics on resolved complaints are submitted regularly, and confidentiality is safeguarded.

The third leg, Regulation 5.3, completes the scheme: a Member also has labour-supplying responsibilities for recruitment and placement services on its territory and for the social security protection of seafarers who are its nationals or residents, enforced through its own system of inspection, monitoring and legal proceedings. Flag, port and labour supply together are what make the Convention effective against a ship whose flag State will not act.

blocks.p: The stem gives you the two headings and nothing else, which is a trap disguised as a gift: candidates write two general essays about 'the flag State is responsible for its ships' and score badly. The marks are in the machinery - the certificate and its periods, the DMLC's two parts, the three-year inspection interval, the four triggers for a more detailed inspection, the two grounds for detention. Write the machinery and the discussion writes itself.

Balance matters. Limb (a) has more material than limb (b) and it is easy to spend twelve marks' worth of writing on the flag State. Sections 2 to 6 are limb (a); sections 7 to 9 are limb (b); stop limb (a) when you reach the complaint procedures.

blocks.h: The idea that organises the whole answer

blocks.p: The flag State certifies; the port State checks the certificate. Everything else follows from that division. It is why the certificate and the DMLC are prima facie evidence, why the port State inspection is limited to reviewing them unless something specific goes wrong, and why the four triggers are all reasons to stop believing the paperwork - it is missing or false, the conditions visibly contradict it, the ship has changed flag to escape it, or a seafarer says it is untrue. Once you see the triggers as 'reasons to doubt the certificate', they are impossible to forget.

ul: Treating MLC port State control as ordinary port State control. Here the officer must accept the certificate as prima facie evidence and is limited to reviewing it unless a trigger fires.
Founding a deficiency on Part B. A port State inspection is limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code.
Saying the DMLC is issued by the flag State. Part I is; Part II is drawn up by the shipowner and then certified.
Forgetting that the certificate ceases to be valid on change of flag and when the shipowner ceases to be responsible.
Writing that the flag State may delegate to a recognized organization and is then discharged. It remains fully responsible.
Giving detention grounds vaguely. There are two: clearly hazardous conditions, or a serious or repeated breach - and an accepted plan of action is an alternative to continued detention.
Omitting Regulation 5.3 entirely. It is not asked, but one sentence showing you know Title 5 has three legs is cheap and reads well.

The edition. At this sitting the operative text is MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2022 amendments do not enter into force until 23 December 2024, five months after this paper. Anything from the 2022 set - and there is a consolidated text carrying it in circulation - is a post-sitting import.
Substantial equivalence does not reach Title 5. Article VI paragraphs 3 and 4 are expressly disapplied to Part A of the Code in this Title. This is a real mark and almost nobody writes it.
Three years is a ceiling, not a period. The inspection interval shall in no case exceed three years; certification drives the actual pattern.

Six months, five years, five months, three anniversary dates. Interim certificate six months; full certificate five years; extension five months; intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. These four numbers are the most examinable facts in limb (a).
Being asked in the oral 'can the port State inspect hours of rest?' Only if a trigger has fired - otherwise the inspection is limited to reviewing the certificate and declaration.
Who draws up each part of the DMLC? Part I the competent authority, Part II the shipowner, certified by the authority or the RO.
Your ship changes flag next week - what happens to the Maritime Labour Certificate? It ceases to be valid; an interim certificate may be issued for up to six months on the change of flag.

What must a port State officer do before detaining? Establish non-conformity on a more detailed inspection and either clearly hazardous conditions or a serious or repeated breach; then either rectification or an accepted plan of action; then notify the flag State forthwith.

A seafarer complains to you as Chief Engineer. What does the Convention require? Handling under the on-board procedures, resolution at the lowest level, no victimization, and his right to go directly to the master or to external authorities preserved.
Where would you find the list of matters inspected before certification? Appendix A5-I - sixteen matters, from minimum age to financial security.

blocks.p: Limb (a) is SYSTEM - DELEGATE - CERTIFY - INSPECT - COMPLAIN: build the system (5.1.1), you may delegate but stay responsible (5.1.2), certify with MLC and DMLC (5.1.3), inspect at not more than three years with independent inspectors (5.1.4), and handle complaints on board without victimization (5.1.5), plus the casualty inquiry (5.1.6).

Limb (b) is ACCEPT - DOUBT - DIG - DETAIN - ESCALATE: accept the certificate as prima facie evidence, doubt it only on one of the four triggers, dig with a more detailed inspection over Appendix A5-III, detain only on hazard or serious or repeated breach, and escalate through the flag State to the Director-General.

blocks.p: The whole of this answer is written from Title 5 of the operative consolidated text, read at source, so the evidence position is strong and there is no unresolved gap. The single live issue is the edition, and it is the reason this question is one of the two decisive temporal exclusions on the paper. The corpus holds two consolidated texts in the same folder: one including the amendments of 2014, 2016 and 2018, and one that also carries the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022. The 2018 consolidation is the operative edition at July 2024, because the 2022 amendments do not enter into force until 23 December 2024 - five months after this sitting. The later text was read only to know what to exclude, and nothing from it appears here. The entry-into-force date itself is carried from the paper anchor rather than from a reading of the instrument, and is flagged accordingly. Separately, no regional memorandum of understanding is named and no detention or inspection statistic is quoted anywhere, because MIW holds no such documentation.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of equal weight with no further sub-structure given. The examiner wants the ENFORCEMENT MACHINERY of Title 5 set out under the two headings, not a general essay on responsibility. Limb (a) is Regulation 5.1 in its five parts; limb (b) is Regulation 5.2 in its two parts, with the acceptance rule that governs both.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 + 8, printed against each limb. Limb (a) carries more material than limb (b), so the discipline is to stop limb (a) at the complaint procedures rather than let it consume limb (b)'s marks.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: Specific machinery with its numbers - the 500 GT threshold, five-year certificate, intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates, six-month interim, three-year maximum inspection interval - and, on the port State side, the acceptance of the certificate as prima facie evidence, the four triggers for a more detailed inspection and the two grounds for detention.

The stem does not mention Regulation 5.3, labour-supplying responsibilities. It is not part of either limb and is given one closing sentence only, so the answer is complete without being off-question
'Port state obligations' could be read as the port State's obligations to seafarers generally; it is read as Regulation 5.2, which is what the Convention itself titles port State responsibilities

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.3 and Standard A5.1.3 (Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC) on the flag State side, and Regulation 5.2.1 with Standard A5.2.1 (acceptance as prima facie evidence, the four triggers and the two detention grounds) on the port State side.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing the answer from the 2022 amendments. At this sitting the operative text is MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 amendments; the 2022 amendments do not enter into force until 23 December 2024, five months after the paper. The second trap is forgetting that substantial equivalence under Article VI is expressly disapplied to Part A of the Code in Title 5.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is SYSTEM (2), DELEGATE (3), CERTIFY (4), INSPECT (5), COMPLAIN (6). Limb (b) is ACCEPT (7), DIG and DETAIN (8), ESCALATE (9).
questions.understand_first: Two States are looking at the same ship for the same purpose, but from different positions. The State whose flag she flies has to build a working system - inspect her, certify her, and stand behind that certificate even when it has paid a class society to do the visiting. The State whose port she enters starts from trust: it must take the certificate at face value and look no further, because if every port re-ran the whole inspection the certificate would be worthless and the ship would never trade. What makes the arrangement safe rather than naive is that trust ends the moment there is a reason to doubt the paper - it is missing or false, what the officer can see contradicts it, the ship has switched flag to escape it, or someone living on board says it is not true. Only then does the port State dig, and only if it finds people in danger, or a breach that is serious or keeps recurring, may it stop the ship sailing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC flag State and port State obligations question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Where Title 5 sits and the substantial-equivalence disapplication. 2 Flag State system. 3 Recognized organizations. 4 Certificate and DMLC. 5 Inspection and enforcement. 6 On-board complaints and casualties. 7 Port State starting position. 8 More detailed inspection and detention. 9 Onshore complaints and Regulation 5.3.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. Sections 2-6 are limb (a) and 7-9 are limb (b); stopping limb (a) at the complaints is what protects limb (b)'s marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the MLC certification periods and thresholds.
retrieval_cards.answer: Certification is required for ships of 500 gross tonnage or over on international voyages, or of 500 GT or over operating from a port or between ports in another country; any other ship on the shipowner's request. The Maritime Labour Certificate is valid for not more than five years. An intermediate inspection falls between the second and third anniversary dates. An interim certificate lasts not more than six months and no second interim may be issued. A certificate may be extended for up to five months.
retrieval_cards.why: Four numbers, each of which is a mark, and all four are examinable in the oral.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who draws up each part of the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance, and what does each contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is drawn up by the competent authority: the list of matters to be inspected, the national requirements implementing the Convention, ship-type specific requirements, any substantial equivalences, and any Title 3 exemption. Part II is drawn up by the shipowner: the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections and the measures proposed for continuous improvement. Part II is then certified by the competent authority or the authorized recognized organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The two-part split is the single most reliable mark in limb (a) and the most commonly muddled.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a port State do before it looks beyond the Maritime Labour Certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: It must accept the certificate and the DMLC as prima facie evidence of compliance, and accordingly limit the inspection to a review of the two documents, except in the circumstances specified in the Code. Any inspection is limited to verifying conformity with the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code - Part B is guidance and cannot found a deficiency.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the rule that distinguishes MLC port State control from ordinary port State control.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four circumstances permitting a more detailed inspection under the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) The required documents are not produced or maintained, are falsely maintained, do not contain the required information or are otherwise invalid; (b) there are clear grounds for believing the working and living conditions do not conform; (c) there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship changed flag to avoid compliance; or (d) there is a complaint alleging specific non-conforming conditions. A detailed inspection must in any case be carried out where the conditions could constitute a clear hazard to safety, health or security, or a serious breach.
retrieval_cards.why: All four are reasons to stop believing the certificate, which is why they unlock the deeper inspection.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what grounds may a port State detain a ship under the MLC, and what must follow?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only two: conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or a serious or repeated breach of the Convention including seafarers' rights. The ship shall not proceed to sea until the non-conformities are rectified, or until the officer accepts a plan of action he is satisfied will be implemented expeditiously. He must then forthwith notify the flag State, invite its representative to attend, request a reply within a deadline, and inform the port State's shipowners' and seafarers' organizations.
retrieval_cards.why: Two grounds and a plan-of-action alternative - the detail that separates a good answer from a generic one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the Convention require of on-board complaint procedures?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fair, effective and expeditious handling of complaints alleging breaches, with victimization prohibited and penalized. Procedures seek resolution at the lowest level, but the seafarer always has the right to complain directly to the master and, where necessary, to external authorities. He may be accompanied or represented, and every seafarer is given a copy of the procedures with the contact details of the competent authority in the flag State and in his country of residence and the name of a person on board who can give confidential impartial advice.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an Appendix A5-I inspected item and the part of Title 5 a Chief Engineer actually operates.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which edition of the MLC applies at a July 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: MLC 2006 as amended through the 2018 amendments. The 2022 amendments, approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session, do not enter into force until 23 December 2024 - five months after this sitting - so nothing from that set may be presented as operative.
retrieval_cards.why: A consolidated text carrying the 2022 amendments is in circulation and reads as current; using it is the specific way this question is failed.

blocks.h: (a) Propeller curves and the safety margins
1. The propeller law, and what a propeller demand curve is

blocks.p: For a fixed pitch propeller working in a given hull and weather condition, the power the propeller absorbs varies approximately as the cube of the rate of revolution, and the torque approximately as the square. Plotted as power against revolutions on the same axes the engine builder uses for the engine, that relation is the propeller demand curve - the locus of every operating point the engine can occupy while driving that propeller in that condition.

The essential point, and it governs the whole question, is that there is not one curve but a family of them. Each hull and weather condition has its own. The reference curve is the light propeller curve, corresponding to a clean hull, calm water and trial conditions - a newly docked ship on a still day. Every deterioration - fouling, roughness, heavy weather, a following sea, shallow water, a damaged or over-pitched propeller, ice, a deep or trimmed-by-the-head condition - moves the curve to the left: the same power is now absorbed at fewer revolutions, or the same revolutions demand more power.

blocks.h: 2. The significance of the propeller curve

ul: It is the matching tool. The engine and the propeller are two machines with entirely different characteristics, and the curve is where they are made to agree. Nothing about propulsion design is settled until the propeller demand curve and the engine's own limits are drawn on one diagram.

It defines the engine's actual working line. An engine driving a fixed pitch propeller cannot operate anywhere on its diagram; it can only operate along the propeller curve. Power and revolutions are not independent variables.

It shows whether the operating point is safe. Drawn against the engine's torque, mean effective pressure and speed limits, it shows immediately whether the engine is working in the region it was designed for or is being driven towards a protective limit.

It is the diagnostic instrument for hull and propeller condition. Because a change in hull or propeller condition moves the curve, comparing the ship's actual power-and-revolutions record against the design curve is how fouling, propeller damage and increased resistance are detected - and how the case for docking or a hull clean is made in figures rather than in impressions.
It is the basis of the margins. The engine is deliberately not laid out on the light curve; the distances between the curves and the layout point are the margins, which is limb A's second half.

It underlies performance monitoring and, now, regulatory reporting. Shaft power, revolutions, fuel index and speed logged against the design curve are what turn a fuel bill into an engineering diagnosis, and the same data feeds carbon-intensity reporting.

For a controllable pitch propeller it becomes a family of curves, one per pitch setting, and the combinator curve is the chosen path across them - which is why a CPP ship can be driven off the intended relation by a combinator setting as easily as by a foul hull.

blocks.h: 3. The engine layout and load diagram - the limits the curve must live inside

blocks.p: The engine builder plots the engine's own boundaries on the same power-against-speed axes. The layout diagram is the area within which the specified maximum continuous rating may be chosen at the design stage, bounded by the maximum and minimum permissible mean effective pressures and the maximum and minimum speeds. Once the rating is chosen, the load diagram gives the boundaries within which the engine may actually be operated:

ul: the maximum speed limit, on the right;

the torque / speed limit, which slopes down to the left and is the binding limit at reduced speed. It exists principally to protect the engine against thermal overload - too much fuel per cycle for the air the turbocharger can deliver at that speed;
the maximum mean effective pressure limit for continuous operation, which binds at high load and speed but is not the limiting boundary at low speed;
the overload limit, available only for a restricted period at sea trials or as the builder permits;
and, at the bottom left, the minimum speed below which the engine will not run steadily.

blocks.p: A heavy-running ship moves up and to the left on this diagram - more torque for fewer revolutions - which drives it towards the torque limit. That is why heavy running is a mechanical problem and not merely an economic one.

rows: Light running margin (LRM)
The horizontal gap, in revolutions, between the light propeller curve and the heavier curve through which the engine is laid out, expressed as a percentage of the layout speed

So that a ship whose hull and propeller have deteriorated, or which is in heavy weather, still reaches full power without crossing the torque limit. A new ship on trials is therefore light running by design
4 to 7 per cent, and up to about 10 per cent in special cases
Sea margin (fouling and weather margin)
The extra power added to the calm-water, clean-hull trial requirement to give the same service speed in realistic service conditions
To cover added resistance from fouling, roughness, wind, waves, current and steering
typically 10 to 30 per cent, historically about 15 per cent
Engine margin (operational or continuous service margin)
The deliberate gap between the service power at which the ship is intended to run continuously and the engine's specified maximum continuous rating
So the engine spends its life at a comfortable load with reserve in hand for schedule recovery, and does not run continuously at its rating
historically about 10 per cent, typically in the range 10 to 30 per cent
Torque / speed limit
The engine's own boundary on the load diagram at reduced speed
Protects against thermal overload; not a design margin but the limit the other margins keep the ship away from
Overload limit and its time restriction
The short-duration boundary above the continuous rating
Available for trials and for the builder's stated period only; not an operating margin

blocks.p: The figures are typical ranges from the engine builder's published project guidance, not requirements, and a particular ship's values come from her own project documents. Two further points earn marks. The margins are not interchangeable - the sea margin buys power, the engine margin buys headroom below the rating, the light running margin buys revolutions - and they are not simply additive in effect. And the sensitivity is worth remembering: about a 20 per cent increase in required power corresponds to only about 1 per cent heavy running. The revolution shift is tiny and the power penalty behind it is very large, which is exactly why the condition is missed on board.

blocks.h: (b) The relation between plant rated output and propeller design power
5. The four points on the diagram

blocks.p: Draw power vertically and revolutions horizontally. Draw the light propeller curve through the origin, and the engine's load diagram boundaries. Four points then have to be placed, and their relative positions are the whole of limb B:

rows: Propeller design point (PD)

The power and revolutions at which the propeller itself is designed - the power required to drive the ship at her design speed in the trial condition: clean hull, calm water, no added resistance. It sits on the light propeller curve
Service propulsion point (SP)
The propeller design power plus the sea margin. This is the power actually needed to hold the design speed in realistic service, and it sits above and to the right of PD
Specified maximum continuous rating (SMCR)
The rating the owner specifies and the engine is built and certified to. It is placed above SP by the engine margin, so that the service point is a comfortable fraction of the rating
The engine layout curve

SMCR is deliberately placed to the right of the light propeller curve by the light running margin, so the engine reaches its rating at slightly higher revolutions than a clean hull in calm water would demand

blocks.p: Stated in one sentence: the maximum rated output of the propulsion plant is deliberately and substantially greater than the power for which the propeller is designed, and it is displaced to higher revolutions as well as to higher power.

ul: Vertically, SMCR exceeds the propeller design power by the sea margin and then by the engine margin. The propeller design power is the ideal-condition requirement; the plant rating is that requirement plus what a real hull in a real sea needs, plus a reserve.

Horizontally, SMCR is displaced from the light propeller curve by the light running margin, so that as the hull fouls and the curve moves left, the operating point moves back towards the engine's layout curve rather than past the torque limit.

The propeller is therefore matched to a condition the ship almost never occupies - clean hull, calm water, trial draught - and the engine is matched to the condition she will actually spend her life in. That deliberate mismatch is the design, not a defect.

The consequence in service. A new ship on trials is light running: she reaches her contract speed at fewer revolutions and less power than the layout point, and the fuel index is low. As the hull fouls the curve migrates left and the ship consumes the light running margin. When the margin is gone she is heavy running, or torque rich: full power now requires the engine to be driven towards its torque limit, the engine is thermally overloaded before it is speed-limited, and the ship can no longer make her speed.

The reverse case is real too. An over-generous light running margin, or a propeller that turns out to be under-pitched, leaves the engine unable to reach its rated power without exceeding its speed limit - the ship 'runs away' on revolutions and never develops full power. Both directions are matching failures.

For a controllable pitch propeller the relation is managed by the combinator: pitch and revolutions are chosen together so the operating point follows a path across the family of curves that keeps the engine inside its load diagram. The same margins are still designed in; they are simply defended by the combinator programme instead of by fixed geometry.

Two limits sit above all of this. The engine cannot be operated above the SMCR except within the overload allowance and for the stated period; and where the engine's power has been limited for regulatory purposes, the effective ceiling is the limited power and the whole matching relation must be read against it.

blocks.h: 7. When the relation breaks down - and what the Chief Engineer does

ul: Recognise it from the diagram, not from the fuel bill. Plot the ship's actual power and revolutions against the design curve. Heavy running shows as an operating point above and left of where it should be: lower revolutions for the same power, higher fuel index, higher mean effective pressure and Pmax, rising exhaust temperatures, falling scavenge air pressure margin, turbocharger working harder and, in the worst case, surging and visible smoke.

Confirm before acting. Check the instrumentation first - a shaft power meter or torsionmeter reading wrongly has sent more than one ship to a hull clean it did not need. Then exclude the environmental causes: draught and trim, shallow water and squat, current, wind and sea state.

Then separate hull from propeller. A gradual, progressive change since the last docking points to hull fouling and roughness; a step change points to propeller damage, a rope or net around the boss, or a changed pitch. Underwater inspection settles it.

Protect the engine while the cause is being found. Reduce power to bring the operating point back inside the load diagram, keep within the torque limit rather than chasing revolutions, watch exhaust temperature spread and turbocharger condition, and do not use the overload allowance to hold a schedule.

Remedy. Propeller polishing and hull cleaning restore the curve; a de-pitched or over-pitched propeller requires a class-approved pitch correction; and persistent mismatch is a technical-management matter, not an engine-room one.

Report and record. Performance data, the diagnosis and the action taken go to the Company through the safety management system and the technical department. The Chief Engineer's authority is to protect the machinery and to establish the facts; the decision to dock, clean or re-pitch belongs ashore, and the engineering case is what gets it made.

blocks.p: Two limbs at eight marks each, and the second is a drawing question in disguise. Limb B says 'using typical engine power versus engine speed diagram and propeller demand curves' - so draw it. A clear sketch with the light propeller curve, the load diagram boundaries and the four points marked earns marks that three paragraphs of prose cannot, and it takes a fraction of the time.

Limb A contains two separate commands. 'Explain the significance' is a reasoning task and 'enumerate the safety margins' is a list task, and both must be done. A script that explains the curve beautifully and then names one margin loses half of limb A.

blocks.h: The one idea behind the whole question

blocks.p: The propeller is designed for a condition the ship almost never occupies, and the engine is rated for the condition she actually lives in. That is the relation limb B asks for, in one sentence. The propeller design point is clean hull, calm water, trial draught. The engine's rating is that power plus the sea margin plus the engine margin, and shifted to the right by the light running margin. Everything else - why a new ship is light running, why fouling makes an engine thermally overloaded rather than merely slow, why the margins are not interchangeable - falls out of it.

ul: Treating the propeller curve as a single curve. It is a family, one per hull and weather condition, and the light curve is only the reference.
Confusing the three margins. Sea margin buys power; engine margin buys headroom below the rating; light running margin buys revolutions. They do different jobs and are not interchangeable.
Saying the engine is laid out on the light propeller curve. It is deliberately laid out to the right of it.
Describing heavy running as an efficiency problem only. It drives the operating point towards the torque limit, which is a thermal protection.
Saying the mean effective pressure limit is what stops a heavy-running engine. At reduced speed the torque/speed limit is the stricter one.
Not drawing the diagram when limb B expressly asks for one.
Quoting a fouling penalty or efficiency-gain percentage that cannot be sourced. The margin ranges given here are attributed engine-builder guidance; a fouling percentage is not, so do not invent one.

'Which comes first, the propeller or the engine?' The propeller design point is derived from the required ship speed in the trial condition; the engine rating is then built up from it by the margins. Getting the direction of the derivation right is the mark.
The light running margin is designed in, not a fault. A new ship that is light running on trials is correct. Saying she is 'over-propelled' is wrong.

The over-generous case. Too much light running margin, or an under-pitched propeller, leaves the engine unable to reach rated power without exceeding its speed limit. Examiners like this because most candidates only know the fouling direction.

The 20 per cent to 1 per cent sensitivity. A very large power penalty shows up as a very small revolution change - which is why the condition is missed and why performance monitoring, not the watchkeeper's impression, finds it.
Instrumentation. Be ready to say that you would confirm the shaft power meter or torsionmeter before condemning the hull.
Where authority stops. The Chief Engineer protects the machinery and establishes the facts; docking, hull cleaning and re-pitching are technical-management decisions ashore.
What is the propeller law? Power varies roughly as the cube of the revolutions and torque roughly as the square, for a given hull condition.
Which limit does a heavy-running engine approach, and why does that limit exist? The torque/speed limit, which protects against thermal overload.
Name the three design margins and say what each buys. Sea margin - power; engine margin - headroom below the rating; light running margin - revolutions.
Where does the propeller design point sit? On the light propeller curve, at the power for the design speed in the trial condition.

Your ship makes her revolutions but not her speed. What do you suspect? Instrument error, draught or trim, current or shallow water, or a propeller problem - check the instrumentation and the environment before condemning the hull.
What would you do before using the overload allowance to keep a schedule? Not use it - reduce power, bring the point back inside the load diagram, and report.

blocks.p: For limb A: ONE LAW, ONE FAMILY, ONE BOX, THREE MARGINS. One law - cube and square. One family - a curve per condition, the light curve as reference. One box - the load diagram with its speed, torque, mep and overload boundaries. Three margins - sea, engine, light running.

For limb B, build the diagram upwards in four steps and say each aloud as you draw: PD on the light curve (design speed, trial condition); + sea margin to reach SP; + engine margin to reach SMCR; shift right by the light running margin to place the layout curve. Then one sentence: rated output exceeds propeller design power, and sits at higher revolutions too.

steps.title: The propeller law, and what a propeller demand curve is
points: Power as the cube and torque as the square of revolutions, for a given hull condition
Not one curve but a family, one per hull and weather condition
The light propeller curve is the reference - clean hull, calm water, trial condition
Every deterioration moves the curve to the left

steps.title: The significance of the propeller curve
points: The matching tool between two dissimilar machines
It defines the engine's actual working line - power and revolutions are not independent
It shows whether the operating point is safe against the engine's limits
It is the diagnostic instrument for hull and propeller condition
It is the basis of the margins, and of performance monitoring

steps.title: The engine layout and load diagram - the limits the curve must live inside
points: Layout diagram bounds the choice of rating; load diagram bounds operation
Speed limit, torque/speed limit, mep limit, overload limit, minimum speed
The torque/speed limit binds at reduced speed and protects against thermal overload
A heavy-running ship moves up and to the left, towards that limit

steps.title: The safety margins, enumerated
points: Light running margin - revolutions - 4 to 7 per cent, up to about 10 in special cases
Sea margin - power - typically 10 to 30 per cent, historically about 15
Engine margin - headroom below the rating - historically about 10 per cent
Torque limit and overload limit as boundaries rather than margins
Typical ranges from builder guidance, not requirements; 20 per cent power to 1 per cent heavy running

steps.title: The four points on the diagram
points: Propeller design point on the light curve - design speed, trial condition
Service propulsion point - PD plus the sea margin
Specified MCR - SP plus the engine margin
The layout curve displaced right of the light curve by the light running margin

steps.title: The relation itself
points: Rated output exceeds propeller design power, and sits at higher revolutions too
Vertically by sea margin then engine margin; horizontally by the light running margin
The propeller is matched to a condition the ship rarely occupies - deliberate, not a defect
New ship light running; fouling consumes the margin; then heavy running and thermal limit
The over-generous case; the CPP case; the overload and power-limitation ceilings

steps.title: When the relation breaks down - and what the Chief Engineer does
points: Recognise from the diagram and the performance data, not the fuel bill
Confirm instrumentation, then exclude draught, trim, shallow water, current and weather
Separate hull from propeller - gradual against step change; underwater inspection
Protect the engine: reduce power, stay inside the load diagram, do not use overload for schedule
Remedy, report through the SMS, and know where the Chief Engineer's authority stops

quick_revision.recall_15s: Propeller law - power as the cube, torque as the square of revolutions. Not one curve but a family; the light propeller curve is clean hull, calm water, trial condition, and every deterioration moves the curve left. The engine's load diagram bounds operation - speed limit, torque/speed limit which binds at low speed and protects against thermal overload, mep limit, overload limit. Three margins: light running for revolutions, sea for power, engine for headroom below the rating. Limb B in four steps: propeller design point on the light curve, plus sea margin to the service point, plus engine margin to the specified MCR, and the whole layout shifted right of the light curve by the light running margin. So rated output is deliberately greater than propeller design power, and at higher revolutions.
critical_numbers: Propeller law: power varies roughly as the cube, torque roughly as the square, of revolutions
Light running margin: typically 4 to 7 per cent, up to about 10 per cent in special cases
Sea margin: typically 10 to 30 per cent, historically about 15 per cent
Engine margin: historically about 10 per cent, typically 10 to 30 per cent
Sensitivity: about a 20 per cent increase in required power corresponds to roughly 1 per cent heavy running
All margin figures are typical ranges from the engine builder's published project guidance, not requirements
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None - this question is engineering and no statutory instrument is relied on. The only regulatory context mentioned is that where an engine's power has been limited for compliance purposes, the limited power is the effective operating ceiling.
quick_revision.major_trap: Confusing the three margins, or saying the engine is laid out on the light propeller curve. Sea margin buys power, engine margin buys headroom below the rating, light running margin buys revolutions - and the engine is deliberately laid out to the RIGHT of the light curve. The second trap is failing to draw the diagram when limb B expressly asks for one.

questions.memory_cue: Limb A is LAW (1), WHY IT MATTERS (2), THE BOX (3), THE MARGINS (4). Limb B is FOUR POINTS (5), THE RELATION (6), WHAT YOU DO (7).
questions.understand_first: Two machines have to work together that behave nothing like each other. The propeller can only take power in one fixed relationship between how fast it turns and how hard it is being driven, and that relationship changes as the hull gets dirty or the weather gets bad. The engine has boundaries of its own - most importantly a limit on how much torque it can produce at low speed without getting too hot, because at low speed the turbocharger is not delivering much air. So the designer draws both on one picture and then deliberately builds in slack. He sizes the propeller for a perfect day - clean hull, flat water - and then rates the engine well above that, and arranges for the engine to reach its rating at slightly higher revolutions than that perfect day would ask for. The slack is there to be used up: as the hull fouls, the ship eats into it. When it is gone she is not just slow, she is being driven towards the limit that exists to stop her cooking her own engine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the propeller curves and margins question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The propeller law and the family of curves. 2 The significance of the curve. 3 The engine layout and load diagram. 4 The safety margins enumerated. 5 The four points on the diagram. 6 The relation between rated output and propeller design power. 7 When it breaks down and what you do.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. Sections 1-4 are limb A, 5-7 are limb B, and limb B must be drawn, not just described.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a propeller demand curve and why is there more than one?
retrieval_cards.answer: For a fixed pitch propeller in a given hull condition, absorbed power varies roughly as the cube of the revolutions and torque roughly as the square; plotted as power against revolutions that is the propeller demand curve. There is a family of them, one per hull and weather condition. The light propeller curve is the reference - clean hull, calm water, trial condition - and fouling, roughness, heavy weather, shallow water or propeller damage all move the curve to the left.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating the curve as a single line is the error that makes the rest of the question impossible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Enumerate the safety margins and say what each one buys.
retrieval_cards.answer: Light running margin - buys revolutions - the gap between the light propeller curve and the engine layout curve, typically 4 to 7 per cent. Sea margin - buys power - added to the calm-water clean-hull requirement to hold service speed in real conditions, typically 10 to 30 per cent. Engine margin - buys headroom below the rating, historically about 10 per cent. All are typical ranges from engine-builder guidance, not requirements.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says enumerate; three named margins with their purposes are the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which limit does a heavy-running engine approach, and why does that limit exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: The torque/speed limit on the load diagram, which slopes down to the left and binds at reduced speed. It exists principally to protect the engine against thermal overload - too much fuel per cycle for the air the turbocharger can deliver at that speed. The maximum mean effective pressure limit binds at high load and speed and is not the limiting boundary down there.
retrieval_cards.why: It is why heavy running is a mechanical danger and not merely an efficiency loss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Build the diagram: where do the propeller design point, service point and specified MCR sit?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller design point sits on the light propeller curve, at the power for the design speed in the trial condition. Adding the sea margin gives the service propulsion point. Adding the engine margin above that gives the specified maximum continuous rating. The whole layout is displaced to the right of the light propeller curve by the light running margin.
retrieval_cards.why: Four steps, said aloud while drawing, are the whole of limb B.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the relation between the plant's maximum rated output and the propeller design power.
retrieval_cards.answer: The rated output is deliberately and substantially greater than the propeller design power, and it sits at higher revolutions as well. Vertically it exceeds it by the sea margin and then the engine margin; horizontally it is displaced from the light propeller curve by the light running margin. The propeller is matched to a condition the ship almost never occupies and the engine to the condition she will actually live in - a deliberate mismatch, not a compromise.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the sentence limb B is asking for; everything else is its consequence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the opposite failure to heavy running, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Too generous a light running margin, or an under-pitched propeller, leaves the engine unable to reach its rated power without exceeding its speed limit - the ship over-revs and never develops full power. It is a matching failure in the other direction, and examiners use it because most candidates only know the fouling case.
retrieval_cards.why: Knowing both directions demonstrates the relation is understood rather than memorised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship appears heavy running. What do you do, and in what order?
retrieval_cards.answer: Confirm the instrumentation before condemning the hull. Exclude draught and trim, shallow water, current and sea state. Separate hull from propeller: a gradual change since docking suggests fouling, a step change suggests propeller damage or a fouled boss. Protect the engine by reducing power to stay inside the load diagram, without using the overload allowance to hold a schedule. Then remedy, and report through the SMS to the technical department, which owns the docking decision.
retrieval_cards.why: Confirm, exclude, separate, protect, remedy, report - and knowing where your authority stops.
