blocks.h: 1. Where these two clauses live, and why that matters

blocks.p: The two halves of this question belong to different contracts, and the marks begin with saying so. The New Jason Clause is a clause of the contract of carriage - it appears in the bill of lading or the charterparty and it governs the relationship between the shipowner and the cargo interests. The 3/4ths Collision Clause is a clause of the hull and machinery policy of insurance - it governs the relationship between the shipowner and his hull underwriter. One decides who bears a loss; the other decides who pays for a liability the shipowner has already incurred.

In the Indian jurisdiction the contract of marine insurance is governed by the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. General average adjustment is not governed by statute at all: it is settled by the York-Antwerp Rules, which are a contractual code and take effect only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them - which is why those documents name the edition. The 2016 edition, adopted by the Comité Maritime International at Beijing, is the current one, and the 1994 edition is still met in older contracts. They are not a convention: they have no entry into force of their own and bind only through incorporation, so the edition named in the contract is the edition that governs.

Under Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. Where there is such an act, the sacrifice or expenditure is shared rateably between all the interests saved - ship, cargo, bunkers and freight at risk - in proportion to their values.

Every element must be present, and the absence of any one defeats the claim: a real peril to the common adventure; an act that is extraordinary, not something the ship was already bound to do; intentional and voluntary, not accidental; reasonable; for the common safety rather than for one interest alone; and there must be a saving of property, because if nothing is saved there is nothing to contribute. Typical acts are jettison of cargo, voluntary stranding, water damage from firefighting, machinery damage sustained in refloating, and salvage, towage and port of refuge expenses.

Separate general average from particular average at once, because that distinction is itself a mark. Particular average is accidental partial loss or damage, and it is borne by the owner of the property damaged alone. General average is a deliberate sacrifice or expenditure for the common safety, and it is shared rateably by ship, cargo and freight. Not everything that goes wrong in a casualty is general average.

Two limits follow, and both are commonly missed. Under Rule C, only such losses, damages or expenses which are the direct consequence of the general average act shall be allowed as general average; loss or damage sustained as a consequence of delay, such as market loss, is not allowed, however real the commercial injury. And under Rule VI, salvage payments are not allowed in general average - special compensation payable to the salvor under Article 14 of the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, or under any similar provision such as SCOPIC, is treated as particular charges and falls outside the adjustment.

Rule D is the rule this question turns on, and it is the one candidates leave out. It provides that rights to contribution in general average shall not be affected, though the event which gave rise to the sacrifice or expenditure may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the adventure; but this shall not prejudice any remedies or defences which may be open against or to that party in respect of such fault. Read it carefully, because it does two things at once. The adjustment still proceeds - fault does not stop the general average being drawn up and apportioned. But the fault is not forgiven: it is preserved as a matter of remedies and defences under the law applicable to the contract. So whether the shipowner actually keeps what the adjustment awards him depends on whether cargo has a defence arising out of his fault - and that is precisely the opening the New Jason Clause was written to close.

blocks.h: 3. The problem the New Jason Clause was written to solve

blocks.p: The problem is a gap between two rules that were made at different times and did not fit together.

ul: By the end of the nineteenth century, carriage legislation - and later the international carriage regime - relieved the carrier of liability for loss caused by the negligence of the master or crew in the navigation or management of the ship, provided he had exercised due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy.

But the courts held separately that a shipowner cannot claim contribution in general average where the peril arose from a fault of his own side. The reasoning was that a party may not profit from the consequences of its own default.

The result was an absurdity. The shipowner was not liable to cargo for the navigational negligence that caused the stranding, yet he could not recover from cargo any part of the extraordinary expenditure he then incurred to save cargo from the consequences of it. He bore the whole of a general average sacrifice made for everybody's benefit.

Shipowners answered this by writing a clause into the bill of lading. An early form was upheld by the courts in the litigation from which the clause takes its name, and the modern form is called the New Jason Clause because it is the successor to that first version.

blocks.h: 4. What the clause does - and what it demands in return

ul: It provides that, in the event of accident, danger, damage or disaster before or after commencement of the voyage resulting from any cause whatsoever, whether due to negligence or not, for which the carrier is not responsible by statute, contract or otherwise, the cargo and the other interests shall contribute in general average with the carrier.

So the operative condition is not that nobody was negligent, but that the carrier is not answerable for the negligence. Where the carriage regime exempts him from liability for negligent navigation, the clause restores his right to contribution.

The protection is conditional and the condition is the shipowner's. The exemption on which the clause depends is itself conditional on the carrier having exercised due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy. A shipowner whose ship was unseaworthy through want of due diligence loses the exemption and with it the clause - so the clause protects the diligent shipowner and does nothing for the negligent one. This is the single most important thing to say about it.
It also secures the shipowner's position on salvage and special charges incurred in the same circumstances.
It is a contractual device and takes effect only if it is in the contract of carriage. It is standard in modern bill of lading and charterparty forms.

rows: Preserves the right to contribution after an incident caused by crew negligence, which is the majority of incidents. Without it the shipowner bears the whole general average alone
May have to contribute even though the shipowner's own crew caused the casualty, which is the outcome cargo interests find hardest to accept and which the clause makes lawful
Makes salvage and port of refuge economics workable. He can commit to a salvage contract knowing the expenditure will be shared
Contribution is assessed on the saved value of the goods, so a valuable parcel contributes heavily even if it was itself undamaged

Puts a premium on provable due diligence - planned maintenance records, class and statutory certification, ISM compliance, crew certification and the machinery history - because the clause fails if seaworthiness fails
Cargo is not released until security is given. In practice an average bond from the cargo interest with a guarantee from its underwriter, or a cash deposit. That takes time and ties up money
He must declare general average promptly, appoint an average adjuster and preserve evidence, because the adjustment will be scrutinised for exactly the seaworthiness point
Delay. An adjustment on a large casualty can take years, and the cargo may be perishable, seasonal or under an onward contract in the meantime
The clause does not protect him from liability for cargo damage; it protects his right to contribution. The two are separate questions
The practical answer is insurance. Cargo policies ordinarily respond to a general average contribution, which is why an uninsured or under-insured cargo interest suffers most

blocks.p: The wider effect is that the clause allocates risk to insurance markets rather than to accident: the shipowner insures his hull and his liabilities, the cargo owner insures the goods and their contribution, and the general average machinery distributes the loss across interests that are all covered. The system only works when everybody is insured, and the party who declines to insure discovers the clause at the worst possible moment.

How much does the cargo owner actually pay? Under Rule XVII the contributory value of each interest is its value at the time and place when and where the adventure ends, determined in accordance with the contract of affreightment and the law applicable to it. Cargo contributes on its value at the time of discharge, taken from the commercial invoice rendered to the receiver or, failing that, from the shipped value; the ship on her value at discharge, from market value or, failing that, insured value; and freight at risk on the amount at risk under the contract of affreightment. That is the figure the security taken before release is designed to protect.

blocks.h: 6. The 3/4ths Collision Clause - what the hull policy covers

blocks.p: The 3/4ths Collision Clause, historically also called the Running Down Clause, is the provision of a hull and machinery policy by which the hull underwriters agree to indemnify the assured for three-fourths of any sum the assured becomes legally liable to pay, and pays, to another party by reason of the insured vessel coming into collision with another vessel. The heads of liability it responds to are, in the standard market form:

ul: loss of or damage to the other vessel, and to property on board her;
delay to, or loss of use of, the other vessel or the property on board her;
general average, salvage, or salvage under contract of the other vessel or the property on board her.
The cover is three-fourths of the liability, and it is limited to three-fourths of the sum insured under the hull policy in respect of any one collision.
Legal costs of defending liability or of taking proceedings to limit it are also borne on the same three-fourths basis, normally subject to the underwriters' prior written consent.

It responds to collision with another vessel only. Striking a berth, a crane, a buoy, a bridge, a lock gate or an offshore installation is not a collision for this purpose - contact with fixed and floating objects falls outside it.

Where both vessels are to blame, liabilities are ordinarily settled on the cross-liability principle: each vessel is treated as paying its proportion of the other's damages, rather than a single net balance being struck. Which basis applies materially affects what the hull underwriter pays, and is one reason the clause is worth understanding rather than memorising.

blocks.h: 7. What it excludes, and where the rest goes

blocks.p: The clause is defined as much by what it leaves out. In the standard market form the collision liability cover does not extend to:

ul: removal or disposal of obstructions, wrecks or cargoes, or anything whatever;
real or personal property other than another vessel and property on board her - which is the fixed and floating object exclusion again;
the cargo or other property on, or the engagements of, the insured vessel herself;
loss of life, personal injury or illness;
pollution or contamination of any real or personal property, other than another vessel with which the insured vessel is in collision and property on board her.

blocks.p: Those excluded heads, and the remaining one-fourth of the collision liability, are the province of protection and indemnity cover - the mutual clubs. So a single collision typically produces two claims from one incident: three-fourths of the ship-to-ship damage from the hull underwriter, and the remaining quarter plus wreck removal, pollution, personal injury and the insured ship's own cargo liabilities from the club. Coordinating those two, and notifying both promptly, is a real operational obligation on the shipowner.

Why three-fourths and not all of it? The uninsured quarter was originally deliberate: leaving the shipowner exposed to a share of every collision liability gave him a direct financial interest in navigating carefully and in defending claims properly, rather than being indifferent to an outcome his underwriter would pay for in full. That is a classic answer to moral hazard. In modern practice the quarter is itself usually insured by the P&I club, so the deterrent largely operates through the deductible, the claims record and the premium instead. Some modern hull forms provide four-fourths cover, and a candidate should say that the fraction is a feature of the policy form rather than a rule of law.

blocks.h: 8. Implications, and the influence on behaviour

rows: Caps and defines the exposure - a stated fraction, of a stated set of heads, subject to a stated limit - so collision liability can be rated separately from hull damage
A gap in cover unless the quarter is placed elsewhere. The first duty is to know where every part of the liability sits, and to arrange the P&I side to meet it
Shares the moral hazard: the assured retains an interest in the outcome, historically through the quarter and today through the deductible and the claims record
Two insurers to notify from one casualty, promptly, and a duty not to admit liability or settle without their agreement. Getting this wrong prejudices the cover
Control of the defence: legal costs are shared but normally only with prior consent, which keeps the insurer in the conduct of the claim
Evidence becomes an asset. VDR data, bridge and engine-room records, alarm printouts, the movement book and photographs decide apportionment - and apportionment decides what is paid
Underwriting reflects the operator's record - management, manning, trading pattern and casualty history
Premium, deductible and renewal terms follow the record, so collision avoidance is a direct commercial return, not merely a safety objective

blocks.p: The behavioural effect, and the part that belongs to the Chief Engineer. Because the shipowner is exposed - through the quarter, through the deductible and through the record - the clause pushes him towards measures that reduce the chance and the cost of a collision: navigational standards and bridge resource management, competent and properly rested watchkeepers, adequate manning, a real passage plan, careful pilotage practice, and prompt evidence preservation after any incident. Most of that is on the bridge. But a very large share of collisions and contacts follows a machinery or steering failure at the wrong moment - a blackout in a channel, a steering gear failure at a pilot station, a main engine that will not go astern, a bow thruster that fails on a berthing. That places the collision-liability exposure squarely inside the Chief Engineer's responsibility: identification and maintenance of critical equipment under the safety management system, the tested reliability of the emergency generator and the changeover, steering gear tests before arrival, main engine astern and blackout-recovery drills, and honest defect reporting rather than deferral. The clause is an insurance provision, but the behaviour it is designed to produce is an engineering one.

Two limbs at eight marks, and each contains three questions rather than one. Limb (a) is what is it - how does it protect - implications for both sides. Limb (b) is what is it - implications for both sides - how does it change behaviour. Every one of those six asks carries marks, and the commonest failure on this question is to define both clauses well and answer none of the four 'implications' or 'behaviour' asks. Give each limb a table for the two-sided part and the balance takes care of itself.

The single most valuable sentence you can write in limb (a) is that the clause only helps a shipowner who exercised due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy. It shows you understand that the clause rides on the carriage exemption rather than standing alone, and almost no script says it.

blocks.h: The idea that makes limb (a) make sense

blocks.p: Two rules were made independently and left a hole between them. Rule one: the carrier is not liable to cargo for the crew's negligent navigation, provided the ship was made seaworthy with due diligence. Rule two: a party cannot claim general average contribution for a peril its own side caused. Put together, the shipowner is not liable for the stranding but must nevertheless pay the whole cost of getting everyone off it. The New Jason Clause closes the hole by contract: if the carrier is not responsible for the cause, cargo still contributes. Say it that way and both the mechanism and the condition follow.

ul: Calling the New Jason Clause an insurance clause. It is a clause of the contract of carriage - bill of lading or charterparty.

Saying it protects the shipowner against his own negligence generally. It operates only where the carrier is not responsible for the cause, which depends on due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy.
Treating the York-Antwerp Rules as law. They are a contractual code, effective only when incorporated, which is why the contract names the edition.
Saying the 3/4ths Collision Clause covers all collision liability. It covers three-fourths, of a defined set of heads, arising from collision with another vessel.
Forgetting the fixed and floating object point. Striking a berth, buoy or bridge is not a collision for this clause.
Omitting the exclusions - wreck removal, pollution, personal injury, the insured ship's own cargo - and where they go, which is P&I.
Answering 'how does it influence behaviour' with one line. It is expressly asked and it is where the Chief Engineer's own material belongs.
Quoting clause wording. Do not. Name the clause and state its effect. A misquoted clause is worse than an accurate description, and no examiner expects a recital.
The seaworthiness condition. Expect 'so does the New Jason Clause help a shipowner whose ship was unseaworthy?' No - it fails with the exemption it depends on.
Cross-liabilities. Where both ships are to blame, liabilities are ordinarily settled on the cross-liability principle rather than as a single net balance. Knowing the term is a mark.

Why three-fourths? The uninsured quarter was a deliberate moral-hazard device. Today it is usually covered by the club, and some forms give four-fourths - so the fraction is a feature of the policy, not a rule of law.
The two-insurer point. One collision, two notifications, and a duty not to admit liability. It is the practical answer an examiner is listening for.

The engineering link. Blackout, steering gear failure and astern failure are collision causes. Being able to connect the clause to critical-equipment maintenance is what makes this a Chief Engineer's answer rather than a lawyer's.
Which contract is the New Jason Clause in? The contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty.

State Rule A. There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
What must cargo do before it is released after a general average declaration? Provide security - typically an average bond with an underwriter's guarantee, or a cash deposit.
Your ship strikes a lock gate. Does the collision clause respond? No - it responds to collision with another vessel. That is a P&I matter.
Who pays for wreck removal after a collision? Not the hull collision clause - it is expressly excluded. The club.

Name three engineering measures that reduce collision exposure. Critical equipment identified and maintained under the SMS; emergency generator and changeover tested on load; steering gear tested before arrival, with astern and blackout-recovery drills.

blocks.p: Limb (a) in four beats: GAP - CLAUSE - CONDITION - CONSEQUENCES. The gap between the carriage exemption and the no-contribution rule; the clause that closes it; the condition of due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy; and the consequences for each side - contribution preserved for the owner, contribution owed and security demanded from cargo.

Limb (b) in four: THREE-FOURTHS - OF WHAT - NOT WHAT - SO WHAT. Three-fourths of the liability and of the sum insured; of damage to the other vessel and property on her, delay and loss of use, and her general average and salvage; not wreck removal, not pollution, not personal injury, not your own cargo, not fixed objects; so what - the quarter, the club, the deductible, the record, and the behaviour that follows.

blocks.p: This is the question on which MIW holds the least source material, and the answer is written to that constraint rather than around it. The marine insurance clause wordings - the New Jason Clause, the 3/4ths Collision Clause and the Institute clause sets - are not held in any form. Both limbs therefore name the clause and explain its effect: nothing is quoted, nothing is paraphrased as though a text had been read, no clause number, paragraph or edition is attributed, and no section of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is cited. The decision that gave the clause its name is identified as the origin of the name, not as a proposition of law read from a report. The general average background is at a better grade and is sourced: the York-Antwerp Rules are held in the corpus, and Rule A and the elements are taken from the MIW built set so that this answer does not contradict the house position. Two further limits are declared. The heads covered and excluded by the collision liability clause are the standard market position; individual policies vary and some modern forms provide four-fourths rather than three-fourths, which the answer says rather than presenting one form as universal. And no quantity is asserted anywhere - no premium, deductible, claims figure or casualty statistic - other than the fractions that are the subject of limb (b) itself.

quick_revision.recall_15s: New Jason Clause - a clause of the CONTRACT OF CARRIAGE. Not fixed objects, not wreck removal, not pollution, not personal injury, not your own cargo - those and the last quarter go to P&I. The quarter was a moral-hazard device; today the club usually covers it and some forms give four-fourths.

quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the New Jason Clause protects a shipowner against his own negligence. It operates only where the carrier is NOT RESPONSIBLE for the cause, and that exemption is itself conditional on due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy - so the clause protects the diligent owner and does nothing for the negligent one. The second trap is treating the collision clause as covering all collision liability: it is three-fourths, of defined heads, arising from collision with another VESSEL only.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is GAP (3), CLAUSE AND CONDITION (4), CONSEQUENCES (5). Limb (b) is COVERED (6), EXCLUDED (7), SO WHAT (8). Sections 1 and 2 set the frame.
questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question are about who ends up paying, and both turn on a deliberate gap. In the first, the law had got itself into a corner: a shipowner was excused from paying for damage his crew's carelessness caused, but was also barred from asking anyone else to share the cost of the rescue that carelessness made necessary. So he paid for the rescue of everybody's property out of his own pocket. The trade fixed that by writing a term into the carriage contract - if I am not answerable for what went wrong, you still share the rescue cost with me - and the courts upheld it. Note what it does not do: it only works while he can show he had done his part in making the ship fit to sail. In the second half the gap is on purpose. The hull insurer pays only three quarters of what the owner owes another ship after a collision, and nothing at all for wrecks, oil, injuries or his own cargo, precisely so that the owner is never indifferent to whether a collision happens. That is why a clause in an insurance policy ends up shaping how the engine room maintains the steering gear.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the New Jason and collision clause question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Which contract each clause lives in. 2 General average in outline. 3 The gap the New Jason Clause fills. 4 What the clause does and its condition. 5 Implications for owner and cargo. 6 What the collision clause covers. 7 What it excludes and where that goes. 8 Implications and behaviour.
retrieval_cards.why: 8 + 8. Sections 3-5 are limb (a) and 6-8 limb (b); the implications and behaviour sections are where most marks are lost.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the New Jason Clause, and which contract is it in?
retrieval_cards.answer: A clause of the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty. It provides that where an accident or danger results from any cause whatsoever, negligent or not, for which the carrier is not responsible by statute or contract, the cargo and other interests shall still contribute in general average with the carrier, and shall bear salvage and special charges incurred.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the right contract is the first mark, and the 'not responsible' formula is the mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the New Jason Clause protect a shipowner whose ship was unseaworthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The clause operates only where the carrier is not responsible for the cause, and the carriage exemption it relies on is itself conditional on the carrier having exercised due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy. Lose the due diligence and the exemption goes, and the clause goes with it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable sentence in limb (a), and almost no script writes it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State Rule A and the elements of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. The elements: a real peril, an extraordinary act, intentional and voluntary, reasonable, for the common safety, and a saving of property.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) cannot be answered without it, and it is examined across the whole MIW set.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to cargo after general average is declared?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is not released until security is given - in practice an average bond from the cargo interest together with a guarantee from its underwriter, or a cash deposit. An average adjuster then prepares the adjustment, which apportions the sacrifice and expenditure across the saved values. On a large casualty this can take years.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the practical implication for the cargo owner that the stem expressly asks about.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the 3/4ths Collision Clause cover, and up to what limit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three-fourths of any sum the assured becomes legally liable to pay and pays by reason of the insured vessel colliding with another vessel: loss of or damage to the other vessel and property on her; delay to or loss of use of her or that property; and her general average, salvage or salvage under contract. It is limited to three-fourths of the hull sum insured in respect of any one collision, with legal costs on the same basis, normally subject to prior consent.
retrieval_cards.why: Three heads, one fraction and one limit - the definitional marks of limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the collision clause NOT cover, and who pays for those?
retrieval_cards.answer: Removal or disposal of obstructions, wrecks or cargoes; real or personal property other than the other vessel and property on board her, so fixed and floating objects are out; the cargo or engagements of the insured vessel herself; loss of life, personal injury or illness; and pollution or contamination other than of the other vessel and her property. Those heads, and the remaining one-fourth of the collision liability, fall to protection and indemnity cover.
retrieval_cards.why: One collision, two insurers - the exclusions are as examinable as the cover.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why three-fourths, and how does that influence shipowner behaviour?
retrieval_cards.answer: The uninsured quarter was deliberate: leaving the owner exposed to part of every collision liability gave him a direct financial interest in avoiding collisions and defending claims. Today the club usually covers the quarter, so the deterrent works mainly through the deductible, the claims record and renewal terms. It pushes the owner towards navigational standards, adequate manning, passage planning, evidence preservation - and, because so many contacts follow a machinery or steering failure, towards critical-equipment maintenance, tested emergency power, steering gear tests and blackout and astern drills.
retrieval_cards.why: The behaviour question is expressly asked and is where the Chief Engineer's own material belongs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the fault of one party destroy the general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Under Rule D of the York-Antwerp Rules, rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties - but this does not prejudice any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds; whether the party at fault keeps what it is awarded depends on the defences available under the applicable law. That gap is what the New Jason Clause closes.
retrieval_cards.why: Rule D is the doctrinal hinge of limb (a) and is the point most often omitted; stating it converts a narrative answer into a sourced one.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The effect of the New Jason Clause, and the heads covered and excluded by the 3/4ths Collision Clause.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW HOLDS NO WORDING OF EITHER CLAUSE, AND NO INSTITUTE CLAUSE SET IN ANY FORM. The anchor directs that this question name the clauses and explain their effect, with no wording quoted and no clause number attributed, and that is what is done. The substance stated is the standard market position and is uncontroversial, which is why this ships as an accepted limitation rather than blocking, but both limbs should be confirmed against a standard bill of lading form and a standard hull policy form before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That collision liability cover is three-fourths, of the heads stated, subject to the limits stated.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the standard market position. INDIVIDUAL POLICIES VARY, and some modern hull forms provide four-fourths rather than three-fourths cover. The answer states that expressly rather than presenting one form as universal. Confirm against the form actually in use before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 governs the contract of marine insurance in this jurisdiction, and no section of it is cited.
reverify_before_publication.why: The Act is named without a section number, as the anchor directs, because no copy is held in the corpus. The identification of the statute is correct at this sitting and is not date-sensitive, but the absence of any section reference is a deliberate limit on the claim and is recorded so a later session does not add one from memory.

blocks.h: 1. Regulation 13 - which engines are caught, and which are not

blocks.p: NOx from ships is controlled by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13. It applies to each marine diesel engine with a power output of more than 130 kW installed on a ship, and to each such engine that undergoes a major conversion on or after 1 January 2000 unless it is an identical replacement. A major conversion means the engine is replaced or an additional engine installed, or a substantial modification is made as defined in the NOx Technical Code, or the maximum continuous rating is increased by more than 10% of the original certification.

It does not apply to an engine used solely for emergencies, to an engine powering equipment used solely for emergencies, or to a lifeboat engine; nor to an engine on a ship trading solely within the waters of her own flag State where that State has imposed an alternative NOx control measure. The Administration may also exclude engines on ships constructed, or converted, before 19 May 2005 trading solely to ports within the flag State.

blocks.h: 2. Tier I, Tier II and Tier III - the limits, and what fixes which one applies

blocks.p: The limits are expressed as the total weighted emission of NO2 in grams per kilowatt-hour, and they depend on n, the rated engine speed in crankshaft revolutions per minute. The tier is fixed by the ship's date of construction, not by the engine's design.

on or after 1 Jan 2000 and before 1 Jan 2011

blocks.p: The two that matter to a Chief Engineer are the last two. Tier II is the global standard and applies everywhere, all the time, to a ship built on or after 1 January 2011. It is achievable by engine design alone - injection timing and rate shaping, injector and nozzle geometry, compression ratio, turbocharging and Miller timing - and needs no aftertreatment. Tier III is roughly a 75% reduction on Tier II at slow-speed rating and cannot be met by engine tuning; it needs selective catalytic reduction or exhaust gas recirculation, or operation on a fuel such as gas in a low-NOx combustion process.

blocks.h: 3. Where Tier III applies - the areas, and the logbook

ul: Tier III bites only inside a NOx Tier III emission control area, and only for ships constructed on or after the relevant date: 1 January 2016 for the North American and United States Caribbean Sea areas, and 1 January 2021 for the Baltic Sea and North Sea areas. For any later-designated area, the trigger is construction on or after the date of adoption of that designation, or a later date specified.
Outside those areas the same ship reverts to Tier II. That is why a Tier III engine is certified to both tiers, and why the aftertreatment can be shut down at sea.

The recording requirement is the one that reaches the engine room. Where an engine is certified to both Tier II and Tier III, or to Tier II only, the tier and the on/off status must be recorded in the logbook or electronic record book prescribed by the Administration on entry into and exit from a NOx Tier III emission control area, and whenever the status changes within one, together with the date, time and position of the ship.

There are narrow exceptions - small recreational craft, and ships whose combined nameplate propulsion power is under 750 kW where compliance is shown to be impossible for design or construction reasons - and a temporary exemption for a ship on delivery, sea trials, or proceeding directly to or from a shipyard inside such an area, provided the engine meets the Tier II limits and the ship does not work cargo.
Do not confuse these areas with the SOx emission control areas, which are a different and longer list. The NOx Tier III areas at this sitting are the four above.

blocks.p: What it is. A homogenizer is a mechanical device fitted in the fuel supply line - typically a high-shear rotor and stator, or a valve through which the mixture is forced at high pressure - which disperses a controlled quantity of fresh water into the heavy fuel oil as very fine droplets, producing a stable water-in-oil emulsion. The water is metered in ahead of the homogenizer; the homogenizer's job is to break it into droplets small enough that the emulsion does not separate before the fuel reaches the injector.

Why it reduces NOx. Almost all NOx from a diesel engine is thermal NO, formed from atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen in the hottest zone of the flame, and its formation rate rises very steeply with local peak temperature. The water carried into that zone absorbs its latent heat of vaporisation and its own sensible heat, and it increases the mass being heated. The result is a lower and flatter peak combustion temperature and a shorter time spent at that temperature, and therefore less thermal NO. The mechanism is temperature, not chemistry - nothing is being converted, the flame is simply being cooled.

Secondary benefits. Each water droplet flashes to steam inside the surrounding oil droplet and bursts it - micro-explosion - which improves atomisation and mixing. That can reduce soot and unburnt hydrocarbon, and it is one reason homogenizers are also fitted purely as fuel-treatment devices, where they additionally disperse the small amounts of water and sludge already present in bunkers and reduce separator losses.

The operational price, which is what the examiner wants. Water in the fuel means lower calorific value per unit mass, so consumption in mass terms rises for the same power. It means higher risk of corrosion in the fuel system and the exhaust path, and of injector and pump wear if the emulsion is unstable or the water is not fresh and treated. It means ignition delay increases, so the engine may need re-timing and may run rougher, and there are limits on how much water an engine builder will accept. Emulsified fuel cannot be stored, so the plant must run on-line and be capable of being bypassed instantly - a homogenizer failure must not stop the engine. And because the emulsion changes the fuel actually burned, its use has to be consistent with the engine's certified condition.

What it is. SCR is an exhaust aftertreatment system: a reactor containing a catalyst, usually vanadium- or zeolite-based on a ceramic or metallic honeycomb, into which a reducing agent is injected upstream. The agent is normally a urea solution, which hydrolyses in the hot gas to ammonia, or ammonia directly. Over the catalyst the ammonia reduces the oxides of nitrogen to nitrogen and water vapour. It is the only aftertreatment that achieves Tier III on a conventional oil-fuelled engine across the full load range.

Arrangement. On a two-stroke engine the reactor is normally fitted before the turbocharger, on the high-pressure side, because the exhaust leaving a slow-speed engine's turbine is too cold for the catalyst to work; on four-stroke and auxiliary engines it is usually fitted after the turbocharger, where the temperature is already high enough. The plant comprises a urea storage tank and heated supply and dosing system, an injection and mixing section, the reactor with its catalyst layers, soot blowers or a compressed-air cleaning arrangement, and a control system taking engine load, exhaust temperature and NOx or ammonia feedback.

ul: Temperature window. Too cold and the reaction does not proceed and, on residual fuel, ammonium bisulphate forms and fouls and corrodes the catalyst; too hot and the ammonia oxidises and the catalyst degrades. Holding the reactor within its window at low load - manoeuvring, port arrival - is the main operational difficulty, and is met by bypassing the reactor, by an exhaust bypass around the turbine, or by heating.
Sulphur. Residual fuel makes the low-temperature limit worse, because more SO3 is available to form bisulphate. Low-sulphur fuel widens the usable window.
Dosing accuracy. Under-dose and the NOx limit is missed; over-dose and unreacted ammonia slips past the catalyst, which is itself a pollutant and produces a smell and deposits.

Consumables and space. Urea must be bunkered and stored heated above its freezing point and is consumed continuously while the system runs. Reactor volume and urea tank capacity are significant design penalties.
Maintenance. Catalyst elements foul, poison and age and are replaced in layers; soot blowing, differential-pressure monitoring and periodic activity testing are the routine tasks.

blocks.p: The practical comparison is with exhaust gas recirculation, which suppresses NOx at source by recirculating cooled, scrubbed exhaust to lower the oxygen concentration and the peak temperature. EGR needs no consumable and no reactor, but it needs a scrubber and water treatment and it affects combustion directly; SCR leaves combustion alone but needs urea, space and a temperature window. Both are ways of reaching Tier III; neither is needed for Tier II.

What it is. Regulation 13 sets the limits but does not say how compliance is proved. Paragraph 8 does that: the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 shall be applied in the certification, testing and measurement procedures for the standards in the regulation. The NOx Technical File is the document required under that Code for each engine. It is prepared by the engine builder, approved by the Administration at the time the engine is certified, and it accompanies the engine throughout its life on board, moving with it if the engine is transferred to another ship.

What it is for. An engine is tested on a test bed under an agreed test cycle, and the certificate says that that engine, in that condition, met the limit. The Technical File is what defines 'that condition'. It identifies the engine and the components, settings and operating values that affect its NOx emission, and it records the permitted range within which each of them may be adjusted or replaced. Stay inside the file and the engine is still the certified engine; go outside it and it is not.

What it broadly contains. The engine's identification - builder, type, serial number, rated power and speed. The identification of the NOx-critical components by their approved part numbers, typically the injection system - nozzles, pumps, cams and injection timing - the turbocharger and charge-air cooling arrangement, the cylinder head and valve timing, and the compression ratio. The allowable adjustment and operating ranges for the settings that affect NOx. The test-bed results and the parent-engine or engine-group data on which certification rested. And the on-board verification procedure to be used at survey.

ul: Why it matters in the engine room. Fitting a nozzle of a different specification, altering injection timing beyond the recorded range, or changing a turbocharger for a non-approved unit takes the engine outside its certified condition. The engine's certificate then no longer reflects the engine, and the position must be regularised by the Administration or the recognized organization rather than by an entry in the maintenance system.

How a surveyor uses it. At survey the engine is verified against the file - typically by a parameter check, confirming that components and settings match those recorded, supported by the engine's own records of adjustments and component changes - rather than by measuring emissions on board.

Regulation 13 backs this with paragraph 9: the measurement procedures are intended to be representative of normal operation, and defeat devices and irrational emission control strategies are not allowed. Auxiliary control devices that protect the engine or facilitate starting remain permitted.

Where an Approved Method is fitted to a large pre-2000 engine under regulation 13.7, that method has its own approved method file with its own verification procedure, and its presence is noted on the ship's IAPP Certificate.

blocks.p: The evidence limit is stated openly: MIW holds the NOx Technical Code 2008 only as an image scan with no extractable text, so this limb is anchored to regulation 13.8, which is read at source, and the content of the file is described as engineering and industry practice. No paragraph of the Code is cited and no Code wording is quoted.

Four short notes at four marks each. The discipline that wins this question is equal time: each limb is worth exactly as much as the others, so a candidate who writes a page on Tier II and III and three lines on the Technical File throws away six marks he already knew. Roughly four to six scoring propositions per limb, in about fifteen minutes each, is the shape.

Limb A is the only one with hard numbers, and the numbers are the marks - the three tiers, the construction dates, the four areas. Limbs B and C are mechanism questions: say what the device does, why that reduces NOx, and what it costs you to run, and all four marks are there. Limb D is the one candidates fear, and it is actually the easiest, because it has a single idea: the file defines the certified condition of the engine.

blocks.h: The idea that ties all four limbs together

blocks.p: Nearly all NOx from a diesel engine is thermal NO, formed from the nitrogen and oxygen already in the air, in the hottest part of the flame, at a rate that climbs very steeply with peak temperature. Every technique in this question is a different answer to that one fact. Tier II lowers the peak by engine design. Emulsion lowers it by putting water where the flame is hottest. SCR gives up on prevention and destroys the NO after it has formed. And the Technical File is what stops the crew quietly undoing all of it by fitting the wrong nozzle.

ul: Saying Tier III applies worldwide. It applies only inside a NOx Tier III emission control area, and only to ships constructed on or after the relevant date.
Confusing NOx areas with SOx areas. The lists are different, and at this sitting there are four NOx Tier III areas.
Saying the tier depends on the engine's build date. It depends on the ship's date of construction.
Writing that water emulsion works chemically. It works thermally - latent heat and added mass lower the peak temperature.
Forgetting that emulsified fuel cannot be stored and that the plant must be bypassable at once.
Placing the SCR reactor after the turbocharger on a slow-speed two-stroke. The gas there is too cold; on a two-stroke the reactor goes on the high-pressure side, before the turbine.
Ignoring ammonia slip and the low-temperature ammonium bisulphate problem - both are exactly what an examiner probes.
Describing the Technical File as 'a file with the engine's papers'. It is the document that defines the engine's certified condition and the permitted adjustment ranges.
Quoting a percentage NOx reduction for emulsion or SCR. Unless you can source it, do not - the marks are in the mechanism.

The logbook entry. Tier and on/off status must be recorded on entry into and exit from a Tier III area and whenever the status changes inside one, with date, time and position. It is the part of regulation 13 that actually lands on the engine-room watch and it is very commonly missed.

130 kW is the application threshold for the regulation; 750 kW is the combined propulsion power below which a Tier III exception may apply; 5,000 kW and 90 litres per cylinder is the Approved Method regime for pre-2000 engines. Three different numbers with three different jobs.
Defeat devices are prohibited under regulation 13.9, but auxiliary control devices that protect the engine or help starting are permitted. Knowing the difference is a mark.
Being asked 'can you switch the SCR off at sea?' Yes, outside a Tier III area, because the engine is certified to both tiers - and the switch must be logged.

Being asked what happens if you fit a non-approved injector nozzle. The engine leaves the condition recorded in its Technical File and the certificate no longer reflects it; the position is regularised with the Administration or the RO.
What are the Tier II limits for your main engine at, say, 80 rpm? Below 130 rpm the limit is 14.4 g/kWh.
Which four areas are Tier III areas? North American, United States Caribbean Sea, Baltic Sea and North Sea.
How do you meet Tier III? SCR or EGR, or a low-NOx gas combustion process. Not by tuning.
Why does water reduce NOx but not CO2? Because it lowers peak flame temperature and thermal NO formation; it does not change the carbon in the fuel burnt.
What is ammonia slip and why does it matter? Unreacted ammonia passing the catalyst, from over-dosing or a cold reactor - a pollutant in itself, and it forms deposits.
Who approves the NOx Technical File, and where is it kept? The Administration, at engine certification; it stays with the engine on board for its life.

blocks.p: One line for the whole question: LIMIT - LOWER IT - CLEAN IT - PROVE IT. LIMIT is regulation 13 and the three tiers. LOWER IT is emulsion, working on peak temperature. CLEAN IT is SCR, working on the exhaust. PROVE IT is the Technical File and the parameter check.

For limb A, remember the two rows that matter and read the third from them: Tier II is 14.4 / 44 n-0.23 / 7.7, Tier III is 3.4 / 9 n-0.2 / 2.0, and Tier I sits above Tier II at 17.0 / 45 n-0.2 / 9.8. Dates: 2000, 2011 for the tiers; 2016 for the American areas and 2021 for the European ones.

blocks.p: Limb A is written from MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13 read in full at source, and the edition was established from the copy's own first page - consolidated as of 1 May 2024 - before any regulation number was asserted. Every limit, exponent, threshold, date and area name is taken from that reading. Limbs B and C are engineering, reasoned from combustion and chemical principles and from standard marine practice, and they are presented as such: no percentage NOx reduction, no fuel-consumption penalty and no urea consumption figure is asserted anywhere, because none can be sourced and a false precision would be worse than an honest mechanism. Limb D carries the one real evidence limit on this question and it is declared rather than disguised: the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 is held in the corpus only as an image scan with no extractable text, and the Annex VI copy read contains no provision naming the Technical File or the EIAPP Certificate. Limb D is therefore anchored to regulation 13.8, which is read at source, and its content is described as engineering and industry practice - no Code paragraph is cited and no Code wording is quoted. The substance is standard and uncontroversial; the grade of the evidence is not, and it is stated.

notes: THE ANNEX VI EDITION WAS ESTABLISHED AT SOURCE BEFORE ANY REGULATION NUMBER WAS ASSERTED, AS THE ANCHOR AT SECTION 6 REQUIRES. The copy read declares itself on its own first page: 'Consolidated version as of 01.05.2024. Includes amendments by resolutions MEPC.328(76), MEPC.361(79), MEPC.362(79)'. 1 May 2024 is TWO MONTHS BEFORE this sitting, so the copy is the correct edition for a July 2024 answer and carries no later amendment.

MEPC.328(76) - the 2021 revised Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022 - is the base revision. MEPC.361(79) and MEPC.362(79) were adopted at MEPC 79 in December 2022 and are carried in the consolidation. All three pre-date the sitting.

THE FOUR NOx TIER III AREAS ARE WHAT THE READ TEXT LISTS, AND NOTHING IS ADDED TO THAT LIST. Regulation 13.6 in the copy read names the North American area, the United States Caribbean Sea area, the Baltic Sea area and the North Sea area. No fifth NOx Tier III area is asserted anywhere.

MEPC 81 (March 2024) FELL FOUR MONTHS BEFORE THE SITTING AND IS HANDLED CORRECTLY. It adopted resolution MEPC.385(81) - read at source for Q3 - which amends MARPOL Annex VI on low-flashpoint fuels and the DCS. That resolution was ADOPTED on 22 March 2024 but is deemed accepted only on 1 February 2025 and ENTERS INTO FORCE ON 1 AUGUST 2025, thirteen months AFTER this sitting. It is correctly absent from this answer, and its absence from the 1 May 2024 consolidation is consistent rather than a gap.

THE SOx SIDE IS TOUCHED ONLY TO MAKE A CONTRAST AND IS CORRECT FOR THE SITTING. The copy read lists five SOx emission control areas including the Mediterranean Sea area, whose designation was in force from 1 May 2024. No SOx limit date is asserted beyond the 0.50% and 0.10% figures in the read text.
MEPC 82 (30 September to 4 October 2024) IS THREE MONTHS FUTURE and nothing is attributed to it.
NO POST-SITTING NOx INSTRUMENT APPEARS. No later ECA designation, no later NOx Technical Code edition and no later amendment set is cited.

THE SOURCE-NOT-HELD ITEM IS NOT A TEMPORAL PROBLEM AND IS RECORDED SEPARATELY. The NOx Technical Code 2008 is unavailable in text at ANY date - the volume held is an image scan with zero extractable characters. Nothing about the July 2024 date makes limb D harder; the corpus simply does not hold the document in a readable form.
NO DONOR, SO NO DONOR CONTAMINATION IS POSSIBLE. Fresh research at P1.
THE INDIAN STATUTE BOUNDARY is recorded as checked and not engaged.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Four independent short notes, equally weighted, spanning the same subject from four directions: the regulatory limit, a combustion-side reduction method, an exhaust-side reduction method, and the certification document that governs the engine's compliant condition. The examiner is testing breadth across a single topic rather than depth in one part of it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. Equal marks means equal writing time. The temptation is to over-write limb A because it has numbers and under-write limb D because it feels administrative; that trade loses marks in both directions.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb A, the tier limits and where each applies, with the construction-date logic correct. For limbs B and C, the MECHANISM - why the device reduces NOx - and its operating consequences, not a description of hardware. For limb D, an understanding that the file defines the engine's certified condition and constrains what may be fitted and adjusted.
primary_source_plan: Establish the EDITION of the Annex VI copy from its own first page BEFORE asserting any regulation number, as anchor section 6 requires
Read regulation 13 in full at source, including the areas, the recording requirement and the Approved Method regime
Confirm whether the corpus holds the NOx Technical Code 2008 in readable form BEFORE writing limb D, and write to whatever that test returns
Assert no percentage NOx reduction, no fuel penalty and no urea consumption figure anywhere
Read regulation 14 only far enough to make the NOx-versus-SOx area contrast correctly
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - the tier limits themselves are stable, but the emission control area list is amendable and the Annex VI edition had to be established at source; a later-designated NOx Tier III area would change limb A.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - MARPOL Annex VI applies through the flag State and through port State control uniformly; the only jurisdictional feature is the flag State's own alternative NOx control measure for domestic-trading ships, which the regulation itself provides for.
technical_ambiguities: The stem writes 'Tier II and III emission regulation on main engine'. Regulation 13 applies by engine power output and ship construction date, not to the main engine specifically; the answer treats the main engine as the example without narrowing the regulation to it

'Homogenizers for water emulsion' could mean a fuel-treatment homogenizer or an emulsion plant for NOx control. The stem's context is a NOx question, so it is read as the latter, with the fuel-treatment benefit noted

The stem prints 'NOX Technical file' with an upper-case X and a lower-case f. The intake reproduces the printed form; the answer uses the conventional 'NOx Technical File' in its own prose without correcting the stem
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six numbered sections. Limb A takes three - application, the three tiers as a table, then the areas and the logbook requirement - because it is the only limb with a regulatory structure to set out. Limbs B, C and D take one each, in the pattern what it is, why it works or what it is for, and what it costs or constrains.

steps.title: Regulation 13 - which engines are caught, and which are not
points: Marine diesel engines of more than 130 kW installed on a ship
Major conversion on or after 1 January 2000, including an MCR increase of more than 10%
Emergency and lifeboat engines excluded; domestic-trading ships under an alternative measure excluded

steps.title: Tier I, Tier II and Tier III - the limits, and what fixes which one applies
points: Limits are total weighted NO2 in g/kWh as a function of rated speed n
The SHIP's construction date fixes the tier
Tier II is the global standard and is met by engine design
Tier III needs SCR, EGR or a low-NOx gas process

steps.title: Where Tier III applies - the areas, and the logbook
points: Four NOx Tier III emission control areas; 2016 for the American areas, 2021 for the European ones
Outside them the ship reverts to Tier II, which is why the engine is certified to both
Tier and on/off status recorded on entry, exit and change, with date, time and position
Narrow exceptions and the temporary shipyard exemption

steps.title: Homogenizers for water emulsion
points: High-shear device producing a stable water-in-oil emulsion
Water absorbs latent and sensible heat, lowering peak flame temperature and thermal NO
Micro-explosion improves atomisation
Costs: calorific value, corrosion, ignition delay, cannot be stored, must be bypassable

steps.title: Selective Catalytic Reduction
points: Urea or ammonia over a catalyst reduces NOx to nitrogen and water vapour
Before the turbine on a two-stroke, after it on a four-stroke
Temperature window, ammonium bisulphate and sulphur
Ammonia slip, urea storage, catalyst fouling and replacement
Compared with EGR

points: Required by the NOx Technical Code, which regulation 13.8 applies to certification and testing

quick_revision.recall_15s: Regulation 13 catches marine diesel engines over 130 kW. Tier by SHIP construction date: Tier I from 2000, 17.0 / 45 n^-0.2 / 9.8; Tier II from 2011, 14.4 / 44 n^-0.23 / 7.7, global and met by design; Tier III inside a NOx Tier III ECA, 3.4 / 9 n^-0.2 / 2.0, needing SCR or EGR. Four areas - North American, US Caribbean Sea, Baltic, North Sea - from 2016 for the first two and 2021 for the last two. Log tier and on/off status with date, time and position on entry, exit and change. Emulsion lowers peak flame temperature; SCR destroys NOx over a catalyst with urea, watching the temperature window and ammonia slip; the Technical File defines the engine's certified condition and its permitted adjustment ranges.
critical_numbers: Application: marine diesel engines of more than 130 kW
Tier I - ships constructed 1 Jan 2000 to before 1 Jan 2011: 17.0 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 45 n^-0.2, 9.8 at 2,000 rpm and above
Tier II - ships constructed on or after 1 Jan 2011: 14.4 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 44 n^-0.23, 7.7 at 2,000 rpm and above
Tier III - inside a NOx Tier III ECA: 3.4 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 9 n^-0.2, 2.0 at 2,000 rpm and above
Tier III construction triggers: 1 Jan 2016 North American and US Caribbean Sea; 1 Jan 2021 Baltic and North Sea
Major conversion: maximum continuous rating increased by more than 10%
Tier III exception threshold: combined nameplate propulsion power under 750 kW
Approved Method regime: engines over 5,000 kW with per-cylinder displacement at or above 90 litres, ships built 1990-2000
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13. Paragraph 13.5.3 is the one that reaches the watchkeeper - tier and on/off status logged with date, time and position on entering and leaving a NOx Tier III emission control area. Paragraph 13.8 applies the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 to certification, testing and measurement, which is where the NOx Technical File comes from.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying Tier III applies worldwide. It applies only inside a NOx Tier III emission control area - four of them at this sitting - and only to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2016 or 1 January 2021 depending on the area. Outside, the same ship reverts to Tier II. The second trap is presenting SCR as a clean fix: unreacted ammonia that passes the catalyst is AMMONIA SLIP, a pollutant in its own right, and ammonia is never to be described as a zero-emission substance. The third is quoting a percentage NOx reduction for emulsion or SCR; the marks are in the mechanism, and an unsourced percentage is worse than none.

questions.memory_cue: LIMIT (1, 2, 3), LOWER IT (4), CLEAN IT (5), PROVE IT (6).
questions.understand_first: Almost all the nitrogen oxide a diesel engine makes is not coming from the fuel. It is made out of the air itself, in the hottest part of the flame, and the amount made climbs very steeply as that peak temperature rises. Everything in this question is a different response to that single fact. The rules set a ceiling that gets lower in steps, and which step you sit on depends on when the ship was built and, for the strictest step, where she is at the time. One method attacks the cause by carrying water into the flame so it burns cooler. Another gives up on preventing it and instead sprays a chemical into the exhaust that turns the gas back into nitrogen and water over a catalyst. And because all of this is proved once on a test bed and then trusted for twenty-five years, the last part of the question is the document that records exactly which components and settings the engine was certified with - so that nobody can quietly undo the compliance with a spare part.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the NOx short-notes question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Regulation 13 application. 2 The three tiers and their limits. 3 Where Tier III applies and the logbook requirement. 4 Homogenizers for water emulsion. 5 Selective catalytic reduction. 6 The NOx Technical File.
retrieval_cards.why: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. Limb A takes three sections because it has a regulatory structure; the other three limbs take one each and must get equal writing time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Tier I, Tier II and Tier III NOx limits and the ships they apply to.
retrieval_cards.answer: Tier I, ships constructed on or after 1 January 2000 and before 1 January 2011: 17.0 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 45 n^-0.2 from 130 to below 2,000 rpm, 9.8 g/kWh at 2,000 rpm and above. Tier II, ships constructed on or after 1 January 2011: 14.4, 44 n^-0.23, 7.7. Tier III, inside a NOx Tier III emission control area: 3.4, 9 n^-0.2, 2.0. All as total weighted NO2, with n the rated engine speed.
retrieval_cards.why: Nine numbers, all quotable, and the highest mark density on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does Tier III apply, and what must be recorded?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only inside a NOx Tier III emission control area, and only for ships constructed on or after 1 January 2016 for the North American and US Caribbean Sea areas or 1 January 2021 for the Baltic and North Sea areas. Tier and on/off status must be logged on entry into and exit from such an area, and whenever the status changes within one, with the date, time and position.
retrieval_cards.why: The four areas and the logbook entry are the parts of regulation 13 that actually reach the engine-room watch.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a water-in-oil emulsion reduce NOx, and what does it cost?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nearly all diesel NOx is thermal NO, formed from atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen at a rate that rises steeply with peak flame temperature. Water carried into the flame absorbs its latent heat of vaporisation and its sensible heat and increases the mass being heated, lowering and flattening the peak temperature. It costs calorific value per unit mass, raises corrosion and wear risk, lengthens ignition delay, and the emulsion cannot be stored - so the plant runs on-line and must be instantly bypassable.
retrieval_cards.why: Mechanism plus consequences is the whole four marks; a description of the hardware alone is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an SCR plant work, and where is the reactor fitted?
retrieval_cards.answer: A urea solution or ammonia is injected into the exhaust upstream of a catalyst; over the catalyst the ammonia reduces the oxides of nitrogen to nitrogen and water vapour. On a slow-speed two-stroke the reactor is fitted before the turbocharger, on the high-pressure side, because post-turbine gas is too cold; on four-stroke and auxiliary engines it is fitted after the turbocharger.
retrieval_cards.why: The placement question distinguishes a candidate who has seen the plant from one who has read about it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the main operating constraints on an SCR plant?
retrieval_cards.answer: The temperature window - too cold and the reaction stalls and ammonium bisulphate fouls and corrodes the catalyst, which is worse on high-sulphur fuel; too hot and the ammonia oxidises and the catalyst degrades. Dosing accuracy - under-dose and the limit is missed, over-dose and ammonia slips past the catalyst. Plus urea bunkering and heated storage, reactor space, and catalyst fouling, poisoning, ageing and layer replacement.
retrieval_cards.why: Low-load operation and ammonia slip are the standard oral follow-ups.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the NOx Technical File and why does it matter on board?
retrieval_cards.answer: The document required for each engine under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008, which regulation 13.8 applies to certification, testing and measurement. Prepared by the builder, approved by the Administration at certification, and accompanying the engine for its life. It identifies the engine and its NOx-critical components and settings, and records the permitted range within which each may be adjusted or replaced. It defines the engine's certified condition: fitting a non-approved component or moving a setting outside the recorded range takes the engine outside that condition.
retrieval_cards.why: The single idea of limb D - it is not a folder of papers, it is the definition of the compliant engine.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does regulation 13.9 say about defeat devices?
retrieval_cards.answer: The measurement procedures in the NOx Technical Code are intended to be representative of normal engine operation. Defeat devices and irrational emission control strategies undermine that intention and are not allowed. Auxiliary control devices used to protect the engine or its ancillary equipment against damaging operating conditions, or to facilitate starting, remain permitted.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction between a prohibited defeat device and a permitted auxiliary control device is a clean, examinable mark.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The contents and function of the NOx Technical File as described in limb D.
reverify_before_publication.why: THE REVISED NOx TECHNICAL CODE 2008 IS NOT HELD IN READABLE FORM. The volume in the corpus is an image scan with zero extractable characters, and the Annex VI copy read contains no provision naming the Technical File or the EIAPP Certificate. Limb D is anchored to regulation 13.8, which is read at source, and its content is stated as engineering and industry practice: no Code paragraph is cited and no Code wording is quoted. The substance is standard and uncontroversial, which is why this ships as an accepted limitation rather than blocking, but it should be confirmed against the Code text before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The NOx Tier III emission control areas are the North American, United States Caribbean Sea, Baltic Sea and North Sea areas.
reverify_before_publication.why: Read from regulation 13.6 of the Annex VI copy consolidated as of 1 May 2024, two months before the sitting. The area list is amendable, and a later designation would change the answer for a later sitting. The figure is correct for July 2024 and must be re-derived rather than reused.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Annex VI copy used is consolidated as of 1 May 2024 and includes MEPC.328(76), MEPC.361(79) and MEPC.362(79).
reverify_before_publication.why: Established from the copy's own first page. It is the fact that makes every regulation number in limb A safe for this sitting, and it is also what confirms that MEPC.385(81) - adopted 22 March 2024 but in force only from 1 August 2025 - is correctly absent. Re-establish the edition before reusing this answer at another sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No percentage NOx reduction is asserted for water emulsion or for selective catalytic reduction.
reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate. PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md section 2.1 requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision, and no sourced figure is held. Recorded so that a later session does not quietly add one.
